v0.3.1 2026-11-14

    Sources, stages, gathers and sinks, each made afresh for a run and
    told how it ended, with words to make them and | to join them.

    Pipelines can be made with pipeline(), and named, and a function
    whose values can be code references can take its stages as a
    pipeline given last. pipeline() is one of the words in
    Ekorn::Pipeline::Factories, short functions that make Ekorn's
    types: stage, gather, source, generator with yield, sink_one and
    sink_many. The README's CPAN badge keeps up with releases, and the
    how-to says where a stage belongs. Stages::Flow has take_first,
    take_last and take_single, and take_if and drop_if, which filter.
    Ekorn::Pipeline::Tooling exports every stage, source, sink and
    word from one module, by tags. Ekorn::Pipeline::JSON reads and
    writes JSON and JSON Lines, as sources, stages or sinks, and
    Ekorn::Pipeline::Sugar names pipelines as the program compiles,
    each with a function of its name.

    A run's parts can be made afresh for it, and told how it ended:
    sources that close what they open, however the run ends; sinks
    that consume every value and give a result, committing only when
    the run is done; and gathers with an end as well as a flush, what
    v0.2.0 called the end function; Sources and Sinks have them
    ready-made, and Operators joins them with |. A part's set-up, or
    a package's role method, can return its parts by name, as a hash
    reference, rather than as a list in a set order. An iterator is an
    object, which can read what's left in one call, end its run early,
    and say how it ended, and which ends its run when it's let go.

    Pushing values through plain subs is several times faster, reading
    an iterator's values in one call a tenth faster, and a stop about
    three times cheaper.

    It ships nineteen roadmap items, 2026-0009, 2026-0010, 2026-0011,
    2026-0013, 2026-0014, 2026-0016, 2026-0017, 2026-0018, 2026-0021,
    2026-0024, 2026-0025, 2026-0026, 2026-0027, 2026-0028, 2026-0029,
    2026-0030, 2026-0031, 2026-0032 and 2026-0034. It changes what
    some code sees, as the entries marked "Changed" say: a gather, an
    iterator, every canned stage, and the stages a pipeline gives back
    are objects, called as code references, not code references
    themselves; a gather's message names the flush and the end; a
    stage's error names the named pipeline it's in; the messages for
    what isn't a stage or a source say what one is; and a pipeline
    named alone, pipeline('clean'), is the pipeline itself, so its
    stages are numbered where it's given. Otherwise, existing code
    runs as before.

    - Ekorn::Pipeline::Sugar names pipelines as the program compiles:
      use Ekorn::Pipeline::Sugar pipeline => {name => [@stages]}, or an
      array of pairs, names each in the package that uses it, and gives
      that package a function of each name, which runs values through
      the pipeline, and, given a pipeline last, through that too. A
      definition can name any other in the same use, in either order.
      Mistakes, such as a name taken already, or a circle of names,
      croak as the use compiles. import_into does the same for a
      package given, for other modules' sugar. Sub::Util, which comes
      with Perl, is a new dependency. (roadmap 2026-0010)
    - Ekorn::Pipeline::JSON makes from_json and to_json, for one JSON
      document, and from_jsonl and to_jsonl, for JSON Lines: each a
      source or a sink given a file or a filehandle, and a stage given
      neither. from_json gives an array's elements, or the document
      itself; from_jsonl gives each line's document, read a block at a
      time, as values are pulled. to_json writes every value as one
      array, and to_jsonl a value a line. As stages, each passes on
      what a file would hold, so to_json and from_json undo each
      other, as to_jsonl and from_jsonl do. The encoder is
      JSON::MaybeXS's, configured by a json option, or replaced by an
      object of the caller's. Tooling exports all four, by a :json
      tag. JSON::MaybeXS is a new dependency. The user guide reads and
      writes JSON in chapters 5 and 6, and walks through how a module
      like it is put together in chapter 10. (roadmap 2026-0034)
    - Ekorn::Pipeline::Tooling exports what callers use to do work,
      from one module, so there's nothing to remember about which
      module makes which: tags :core (Stop and gather), :flow, :batch
      and :taps, :stages for the three, :sources, :sinks, :words (the
      factories) and :all. Each tag holds every name its module
      exports, as the same sub, and nothing is exported by default.
      It leaves out is_stage, is_sink and croakf, which are for
      extending the package, and the operators, which stay a pragma.
      The user guide's examples, the README's and the reference's
      At a glance import from it. (roadmap 2026-0031)
    - The reference has a section, Making each kind of part, for
      developers: a table of what each piece of a part, its set-up,
      step, flush, end and context, is called with, returns, and
      whether it may stop the run, and a worked example of each kind
      of part, made with a word and as a class, from a stage with
      state to an object that's both a source and a sink, committing
      only a run that went through. Every example in the README, the
      user guide, the reference and the modules' POD writes a
      pipeline of two or more stages a stage to a line, and
      paragraphs are filled evenly again.
    - The role methods, by which any object can be a source, a stage
      or a sink, are named in capitals, EKORN_SOURCE, EKORN_STAGE,
      EKORN_SINK_ONE and EKORN_SINK_MANY, as Perl names subs that its
      runtime calls, not their caller, such as DESTROY, and as CPAN
      names hooks for another package, such as TO_JSON. No release had
      them in lower case (roadmap 2026-0027).
    - A set-up, a gather's, a source's or a sink's, and a role method,
      EKORN_SOURCE, EKORN_STAGE, EKORN_SINK_ONE or EKORN_SINK_MANY,
      can return its parts by name, as a hash reference with the keys
      step, flush, end and context, giving only those it has, in place
      of a list in a set order with undef for one left out before one
      given: gather { {step => $step, end => $end} }. Other keys are
      ignored, and a hash without what its part needs croaks, as a
      list does. The list still works. Ekorn's own sources, sinks and
      stages, and an iterator's EKORN_SOURCE, return theirs by name

      Perl, none exported by default: from_array(@values); from_fh($fh),

      I/O layers given, if any, for each run, and closed however it
      ends; and counter($start, $step), without end. With $/
      undefined, from_fh and from_file slurp, an empty file giving
      none. (roadmap 2026-0016)

      $stage a source, and @{ $source } every value, read through. A
      chain starts with a source or a stage made with a word, never a

      scope, they croak "Expected use Ekorn::Pipeline::Operators in

v4.2.0 2026-11-26

    The README, the user guide and the reference each come in two
    parts, DBIx::Squirrel first, then what Ekorn::Pipeline adds.
    DBIx::Squirrel::Tooling's tags hold lists of its own, so a newer
    Ekorn::Pipeline changes nothing a caller imports. Three names come
    in: is_stop, which tells a stop from any other error; is_stage, in
    Tooling's :core; and $DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Taps::DumpSecrets,
    dump_to's setting by DBIx::Squirrel's name.

    It ships roadmap 2026-0052 to 2026-0056, and 2026-0058 to 2026-0063.
    Requires Ekorn::Pipeline >= v0.4.3, < v0.5.0, which gives a
    pipeline's iterator its next.

    - Why. Ekorn::Pipeline began as DBIx::Squirrel's pipeline, and
      moved into a distribution of its own in 2026, as it was useful,
      and usable, well beyond database rows. The documents went on
      telling DBIx::Squirrel's story in its words: keep_all, one of
      Ekorn::Pipeline's sinks, appeared 29 times in the guide and 25 in
      the reference, and the README used it more than the iterator's
      own all. So a reader had to learn both libraries to follow
      either, and the two read as one. The separation the split began
      is only now being completed, in the documents first (roadmap
      2026-0052, 2026-0053).
    - Part 1 of each document is DBIx::Squirrel, complete in itself:
      placeholders, the iterator and stages, on handles that are still
      the DBI's, ending where a reader may stop. It opens with what
      DBIx::Squirrel is, said without Ekorn::Pipeline, and shows its
      gains beside plain DBI. Results come from the iterator's own
      methods. An author test keeps Ekorn::Pipeline's names out of it.
    - Part 2 is a different job, data crossing the database's edge:
      query results written to files, JSON and CSV, loaded from them
      in batches, or sent to several places in one run. It opens, in
      the guide, with why the two split, and shows the two working
      together: a function written in Part 1's terms takes Part 2's
      sinks unchanged (roadmap 2026-0054 to 2026-0056).
    - Each example in the guide and the reference imports what it
      uses, from the module that makes it, so it works when copied.
      An author test checks it.
    - The guide's account of a missing bind value is corrected: plain
      DBI fails when a ? has no value, and binds NULL, without a word,
      only for a placeholder bound by name with bind_param. It gains a
      JSON recipe, and explains a pipeline's iterator.
    - DBIx::Squirrel::Tooling's tags hold lists of its own. What a tag
      of Ekorn::Pipeline's names holds, such as :sinks, was whatever
      Ekorn::Pipeline::Tooling's held, so a name Ekorn::Pipeline added
      in a v0.4.x failed t/28-tooling.t as DBIx::Squirrel installed
      beside it, and needed a release of ours. Now a name it adds
      comes into a tag only in a release of DBIx::Squirrel that adds
      it, and one it drops fails as Tooling loads. A caller imports
      the same names as before (roadmap 2026-0059).
    - is_stop, from DBIx::Squirrel::Stop on request, and in Tooling's
      :core, is true of a stop, however it was thrown, and false of any
      other error, so a stage that catches errors can pass a stop on
      without naming its class, Ekorn::Pipeline::Stop. The guide's and
      the reference's catch examples use it (roadmap 2026-0060).
    - DBIx::Squirrel::Tooling's :core holds is_stage, Ekorn::Pipeline's,
      so a function finding the stages at the end of its arguments
      imports it from DBIx::Squirrel, as the reference now shows.
      Tooling had left it out as for extending, not using (roadmap
      2026-0061).
    - $DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Taps::DumpSecrets, true, has dump_to
      write each value in full, without redacting secrets. It's
      Ekorn::Pipeline's setting under DBIx::Squirrel's name, tied to
      it, so local on either sets both, as callers set Data::Dumper's
      (roadmap 2026-0062).
    - Requires Ekorn::Pipeline v0.4.3 or later, below v0.5.0, where it
      was v0.4.0: its iterator has next, as DBIx::Squirrel's has, so the
      guide shows one loop that reads either, and the reference's
      examples use it. The guide's Part 2 links to Ekorn::Pipeline's
      new way in for readers coming from DBIx::Squirrel (roadmap
      2026-0063).

v2.0.5 2026-11-08

    The successor to 1.6.5: a rewrite in modern Perl.

    The reference and the how-to ship as POD manuals, so MetaCPAN and
    perldoc have them with the modules (roadmap 2026-0001).

    Code written for 1.x needs changes to run. "Upgrading from 1.x", in
    DBIx::Squirrel::Manual::Reference, lists them. To stay on 1.x, which
    supports older Perls, install its last version:
    cpanm DBIx::Squirrel@1.6.5. Its code is archived at
    https://github.com/nukopian/DBIx-Squirrel-1.

    - Requires Perl 5.36 or later. Compress::Bzip2, Crypt::CBC, Dotenv,
      JSON::Syck and YAML::Syck are no longer dependencies, and loading
      the module no longer reads a .env file.
    - Placeholders in the styles ?, ?1, :1, $1, :name and $name, one
      style to a statement, each rewritten as ? for the DBI. Quoted
      strings and identifiers, comments, casts and PostgreSQL's
      dollar-quoted bodies are left alone, read by the database's rules;
      the ekorn_dialect attribute names the database behind DBD::ODBC
      or DBD::Proxy. DBD::Pg's placeholder options are followed.
      Comments are passed on to the database, where 1.x removed them.
    - A numbered or named placeholder takes one value wherever it
      appears. Numbers are written in the digits 0-9: a digit of another
      script is part of a name, there and in get_column, pluck and
      bind_param, rather than read as 0. Named values come as pairs or
      in a hash reference, with or without the sigil, and an array
      reference stands for the values in it. Values that don't match
      the placeholders croak, and so does executing a statement with
      some left unbound.
    - A placeholder with "..." before it, such as ...:ids or ...?, takes
      a list, written as a ? for each of its values, for IN and anywhere
      else SQL takes a list. The statement is prepared with its values,
      by do, the select methods, iterate, results and Sugar's functions;
      prepare and prepare_cached croak given one, and so do an empty
      list and a list holding a reference. To a statement whose one
      value is a list, a single array reference is the list. An
      iterator's reset prepares the statement again for a list of
      another length.
    - A statement can be a string, lines in an array reference, a code
      reference returning either, or a statement handle.
    - do and the select methods take bind values without the
      attributes in front. do returns what the DBI's do returns, in any
      context: 1.x also returned the statement handle in list context.
    - connect and prepare croak if they fail, whatever RaiseError says.
      connect clones a database handle given in place of a data source.
    - Errors, and the DBI's warnings, are reported at the line that
      called DBIx::Squirrel, naming the method called, as plain DBI
      reports them.
    - iterate returns a DBIx::Squirrel::Iterator, replacing
      DBIx::Squirrel::it, with next, all, single, reset, count, column_names and
      sth, and no aliases. next no longer sets $_, and single croaks on a
      second result, where 1.x warned. Rows are fetched 100 at a time,
      in the shape the ekorn_slice attribute gives, replacing slice,
      cache_size and their defaults; all, without stages, fetches the
      rest at once, close to the DBI's own speed. column_names gives the
      statement's column names, read when it's executed, as DBD::mysql
      gives none once the last row is fetched.
    - Stages, 1.x's transformations, follow the bind values. Each takes
      a value as its argument and in $_, and returns nothing to drop it,
      one value, or several. Stop, from DBIx::Squirrel::Stop, ends a
      pipeline early, and DBIx::Squirrel::Context gives a stage its
      iterator, result_number and result_original.
    - DBIx::Squirrel::Pipeline runs any values through stages, and pipe
      and tap run a database or statement handle through them.
      A pipeline's stages method returns its stages, to give wherever
      stages go, with more after them.
    - Once a stage dies, an iterator or result set has ended: next and
      all return nothing more, and the statement is finished; reset
      runs it again from the start.
    - gather, from DBIx::Squirrel::Gather, makes a stage afresh for each
      run of its pipeline, from a block returning the stage and,
      optionally, a function called once the values run out, whose
      values go through the rest of the stages. A stage can batch rows,
      make one value from all of them, or keep a count that starts
      again on each execution.
    - Canned stages, each module exporting its usual ones:
      DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Flow's take and drop, with take_while and
      drop_while on request; DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Rows's pluck and
      as_hash, for rows of any shape; DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Batch's
      batch and collect, passing values on in batches, or all at once;
      and DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Taps's peek and count_into, with
      dump_to on request, looking at values as they go by.
    - The pipeline is Ekorn::Pipeline, a distribution of its own, which
      began here, and which DBIx::Squirrel requires, from v0.1.1 up to,
      but not including, v0.2.0. DBIx::Squirrel::Pipeline, Stop, Gather
      and Pipes, and the stages in DBIx::Squirrel::Stages::Flow, Batch
      and Taps, are DBIx::Squirrel's names for its modules, and stay:
      each is a subclass of Ekorn's, or exports Ekorn's functions, from
      a list of its own. A stage that catches errors throws a stop on if
      it isa Ekorn::Pipeline::Stop, which every stop is, including those
      the canned stages throw.
    - results returns a DBIx::Squirrel::Results, replacing
      DBIx::Squirrel::rs, whose rows are DBIx::Squirrel::Result objects,
      replacing DBIx::Squirrel::rc: one class for each list of column
      names, with a method for each column, in lower case. get_column
      takes a name or a position, and the ekorn_result_class attribute
      sets the rows' base class.
    - DBIx::Squirrel::Sugar replaces database_entities: a function for
      each database, connected when it's first used, and for each
      statement, with stages of its own.
    - prepare_cached keeps apart statements rewritten the same, such as
      SELECT :a, :b and SELECT :b, :a, and never hands out a handle an
      iterator is part way through.
    - The ekorn_finish_active attribute finishes a statement still
      active before executing it again.
    - Attributes starting ekorn_ aren't passed on to the DBI. Given to
      connect, they're the defaults for every statement the handle
      prepares.
    - use DBIx::Squirrel takes the names the DBI exports, such as
      :sql_types, as use DBI does.
    - The reference and the how-to ship as POD,
      DBIx::Squirrel::Manual::Reference and DBIx::Squirrel::Manual::HowTo,
      made from their Markdown, so MetaCPAN and perldoc have them with
      the modules (roadmap 2026-0001).
    - SECURITY.md says how to report a vulnerability, privately, and
      CONTRIBUTING.md how to report a bug or ask for a feature; the
      distribution takes issues, not pull requests.
    - Gone, as out of scope: DBIx::Squirrel::Crypt::Fernet, the
      DBIx::Squirrel::Transform modules for JSON and YAML, load_tuples,
      and the file and encoding helpers in DBIx::Squirrel::util. Those
      for Data::Dumper and IO give way to dump_to and peek.

 - glmer() fits generalized linear mixed models, lme4::glmer() and
   glmer.nb(): a binomial (logit), Poisson or negative-binomial (log)
   response with lmer()'s random effects and formula, offset() terms,
   offset and weights arguments, and glm()'s rate and odds ratios (exp)
   with their Wald intervals. It is lme4's method: the Laplace
   approximation, penalized IRLS for the conditional modes, and lme4's two
   stages (the covariance parameters with the fixed effects inside the
   IRLS, then everything), each by Nelder-Mead and a Newton polish on
   Richardson differences, as lmer() fits. Standard errors are lme4's
   vcov.merMod(use.hessian = TRUE), from the Hessian of the deviance.
 - nAGQ from 2 to 100 fits a single scalar random effect by adaptive
   Gauss-Hermite quadrature, with nodes computed at the NV's width, and
   nAGQ => 0 stops after lme4's first stage. family => 'negbin' is
   glmer.nb(): theta starts from MASS::theta.ml() on a Poisson fit, as
   lme4 starts it, and is then estimated with the rest, where lme4
   optimize()s it to 5e-5 on the log scale; theta => holds it fixed.

   levels is practical; several are one dense matrix, factored at every
   IRLS step, which is quick at 71 random effects and took 13 minutes at
   584 (grouseticks' three crossed factors), where lme4's sparse Cholesky
   takes about a second; more than 1000 croaks (lmer() takes 4000). As in
   lme4 (glFormula's allow.n), a grouping factor may have a level per
   row.

   defaults are not: its penalized IRLS stops on a relative change of
   1e-7 in the penalized deviance, which leaves cbpp's log-likelihood
   2.8e-4 below the optimum and its standard errors 0.5% out, and it
   factors log|L|^2 with the working weights of the step before the mode,
   which no setting of tolPwrss removes (1.1e-5 in the deviance on
   grouseticks). glmer() takes the weights at the mode, as the Laplace

 - lm() now takes offset() terms, as R's lm does. It fits the response less
   the offset; fitted_values include the offset, residuals are the response
   less the fitted values, and r_squared and the F statistic are
   summary.lm()'s, which take the offset out of the fitted values first.
   The expressions come back in offset_terms, and predict() adds them, as
   R's predict.lm() and predict.glm() do. Through 0.3427 lm(y ~ x +
   offset(z)) croaked "cannot evaluate term".

   the start or after a `+`. It is a variable of the formula's algebra: a
   term that holds it is dropped (`cnt ~ x + offset(z)*a` is x and a), and
   `cnt ~ x - offset(z)` still has the offset. Each distinct offset() counts
   once, where `offset(z) + offset(z)` used to add it twice. An offset
   expression with a bare operator (`offset(u/2)`, `offset(-z)`,
   `offset(u+z)`, `offset(u-z)`) is evaluated as arithmetic; it used to be
   looked up as a column of that name, and every row dropped. glm(), anova(),
   aov(), zerotrunc(), hurdle(), svyglm() and coxph() read it the same way.

   does: `log(y) ~ .` omits y, `I(y + x) ~ .` omits y and x, and
   `log(y) ~ . - x` leaves the rest. It used to omit only a column equal to
   the whole response text, so `log(y) ~ .` regressed log(y) on y.

   terms. Each `+` rebuilt the whole list and charged it, and the parse was

   y ~ v1 + ... + v8000 parses in a fraction of a second.
 - A formula of a hundred thousand unary minus signs no longer overflows the
   C stack and kills the process; the signs are read in a loop.
 - A trailing operator (`y ~ x +`, `y ~ x + z +`, `y ~ +`, `y ~ 1 +`) croaks
   "the formula has an operator with no operand", as the 0.3426 notes say; a
   cleanup meant for the `+` an intercept marker leaves behind had been
   deleting it. `y ~ x z` and `y ~ x, z` were read as the one name `xz` after
   whitespace was stripped, and are now syntax errors.
 - Comparison and logic characters inside I() (`I(x > 0)`, `I(x == 0)`,
   `I(a == "a")`, `I(x & z)`, `I(x %% 2)`, `I(!x)`) croak "cannot evaluate
   term". R makes them logical factors, which this does not code; they used
   to report "0 degrees of freedom".
 - A column the data lack, in the response, a term, a function's argument or
   an offset, croaks "object 'q' not found", as R's does, naming the column,
   instead of "0 degrees of freedom". An unbalanced offset( reports
   "unbalanced parentheses in offset()" as before.
 - Without an intercept the factor coded by indicators for every level
   is now the one R picks: the first factor of two or more levels in the
   first term that has one (model.c, modelmatrix()). Before, a factor
   counted as full only when its margin was empty, so `y ~ x + b:x - 1`,
   `y ~ x/a - 1`, `y ~ x + z + b:x - 1`, `y ~ x + (x2:z/a) - 1` and
   `y ~ x + a:b - 1` fitted different columns from R's (x, x:bu and x:bv,
   the last aliased, for the first). The margin rule is R's TermCode(),
   whose empty margin is present with or without an intercept.
 - A factor crossed with itself is the factor, as in R: `a*a`, `a:a`,
   `c + c*c` and `(a + b)^3` with a repeated factor gave all-NaN product
   columns; they now give `a`. A term that becomes equal to an earlier
   one is dropped. A numeric variable's repeat is unchanged (`wt:wt` is
   `wt` squared, as the README says).
 - Coefficient, term, level and group_stats names are perl characters
   when the data are: a column found through its UTF-8 spelling, or a
   cell with the UTF-8 flag. With `use utf8` and a column "café",
   $fit->{coefficients}{"café"} now exists, and a level "ж" is no longer
   named `gÐ¶`. This covers coefficients, terms, xlevels, vcov, summary,
   confidence intervals, anova and aov row names, vif and the
   model-frame fitters. A script without `use utf8` gets the same bytes
   as before.
 - A design too wide to fit is refused, before anything large is
   allocated, with "design too wide (more than N columns ...)". X'X
   and the packed factor were allocated at p*p and p(p-1)/2 before the
   degrees of freedom were looked at, so `(v1+...+v30)^4` on 50 rows,
   32 640 columns, was killed for memory. The limit is 2 GiB for the two,
   about 13 000 columns for a double and 9 400 for a long double or
   __float128; R fits such models with NA coefficients, so this is a
   difference, now in the README.

 [Bug fixes: predict()]

 - predict() no longer croaks "newdata is missing column 'log(x)'" for a
   function of a numeric crossed with a factor (`y ~ g*log(x)`,
   `exp(x):a`, `sqrt(u):a`): only plain column names are looked up, and a
   call is evaluated. A factor level holding a ':' (the level "q:r")
   no longer makes every interaction predict NaN; the coefficient name
   is split at the ':' that separates components, not at every one.

   byte E9 where `keys %h` gives the character. Now fixed in colnames() and
   everything built on it (melt's `variable` column, the keys fillna() and
   bfill() add to the rows of a hash of hashes, summary()'s labels, which
   printed a bare E9, and table_one()'s), the outer keys of select_cols,
   drop_cols and rename_cols on a hash of hashes, the columns drop_cols and
   rename_cols keep, both levels of transpose(), p_adjust(), filter() on a

   frame, and dropna($hoa, cols => []) died "Can't use an undefined value as
   an ARRAY reference" on one; a non-array column died "Can't use string".
   Both now behave as cols => ['a'] does: an undef column is all undef, the
   frame is untouched, and a non-array column dies naming it.

   IV on the caller's own SV, so the variable cells came out POK|IOK

   the README says and pandas' linear ignores the index (index, values and

   least N numeric anchors"; and spline/polynomial with an order outside the
   IV range (1e30, inf) report the order given, not "got -1".

   A NaN is now R's NA: left out of the statistics and counted in a
   trailing "NA's" column that appears when a variable has one.
   summary([1,'NaN',3,'Inf']) gives 3 values, Min 1, Median 3, Mean Inf,

 [Bug fixes: binom_test()]

 - An integer count is read exactly. A count held as an IV or UV, or a
   string spelling an integer, no longer goes through an NV, so on a double
   perl binom_test(4503599627370497, 9007199254740991, alternative =>
   'less') answers (R does) instead of croaking "x must be a nonnegative
   integer": v + 0.5 rounds to even from 2**52. binom_test(9007199254740993,
   9007199254740993) returned a statistic and parameter of
   9007199254740992 and 499999999999999000 came back as 499999999999998976,

   to IV_MAX; both are exact now. A non-integer number is still rounded

   is 9223372036854775806)" on a double perl, because (NV)IV_MAX rounds to

 - dbinom(), pbinom(), qbinom(), rbinom(), fisher_test(), mcnemar_test() and
   prop_test() were checked for the same flaw. They take their counts as NVs
   by R's design and return NVs, so there is nothing to lose; fisher_test()

 [Bug fixes: density()]

 - n is rounded up, as R's seq.int(length.out = n) rounds it: n => 1.5 gives
   2 points, 2.5 gives 3, and 0.5 gives 1 where it croaked. It was read with
   SvIV(), which truncated, and on a perl with 32-bit integers n => 2**31
   and 2**32 wrapped into "'n' must be at least 1" instead of "'n' is too

 [Accuracy]

 - The incomplete beta behind pbinom(), pt(), pf() and qf() formed lambda
   = (a + b) y - b with a rounded product, which cost sqrt(n) epsilon at
   shapes of 1e13: pbinom(1765184560411, 17785315992617,
   7151671909757000 * 2**-56, lower = FALSE) was 0.0111407611194407633 on
   a long double perl for 0.0111407611194404998 (2.4e-14 relative). It is
   now a fused multiply-add (nv_fma, fmal in the long-double link probe in
   dist.ini and Makefile.PL) with the rounding error of a + b taken out,
   and the result is 5e-18 off. A long-double libm without fmal keeps the
   old form. Over 8000 mpmath-checked pf/pt/pbinom cases the double and
   long double results are as good as before or better, except one pbinom
   tail of 1.6e-15 whose error went from 1.6e-14 to 7e-14 relative; the
   __float128 results are unchanged. pf near the mean at df ~ 1e12, where x
   and y are already rounded separately, is not fixed and is the same in R.

 [Speed]

 - csort() on a hash of arrays rebuilt each column with av_fetch(), newSVsv()
   and av_push() per cell. A column that is not magical is now read through
   AvARRAY() and written into a pre-extended array; a magical column or cell
   takes the general path, with the array and cell held across the FETCH.
   The same cell copy serves the AoA and AoH outputs, and the arrays being
   built are owned while they are filled, so a croak in a FETCH frees them.
   1e6 rows x 5 columns, HoA to HoA, fastest of 5 fresh processes: 0.631 s ->
   0.392 s; peak RSS delta unchanged at 70 MB.
 - qcut() called a Perl closure per element to find NaN/undef cells; the test
   is now written out in the three loops. 1e6 values: 0.185 s -> 0.110 s,
   peak RSS delta 7.6 MB either way.
 - read_table() reads an archive's central directory once per call and
   reuses it for every member lookup. A workbook of 5,000 worksheets read
   in 6.8 s, quadratic in the sheet count, and reads in 0.32 s.
 - qt() in the far tail grew its bracket by doubling: 16384 steps on a
   __float128 perl for qt(1e-300, 0.01), which is -Inf, 102 ms against
   48 us on a double. The bracket now grows by squaring and stops at the
   first point where the tail is still above the target, so that case is
   0.4 ms there and qt(-1e5, 1e3, log_p => 1), whose answer is 1e43,
   went from 1.1 ms to 0.2 ms. qf() and pbinom() on __float128 remain
   slow: they are 130 bisection steps and one soft-float incomplete beta.
 - lm_design_build() ordered terms by looping to the formula's total
   component count, not to its largest degree: `v1*...*v14` took 1.9 s
   in this step alone and four times as long for each variable added.
   It loops to the largest degree, and the margin search starts at the
   first term that can hold the margin. `v1*...*v13` fits in 0.40 s
   where it took 0.52 s; the rest of that time is the formula algebra.

0.3426 2026-11-19 CST 

 [Behavior change: read_table() of an .xlsx]

 - read_table() now returns the text of an .xlsx as perl characters, not
   as the raw UTF-8 bytes of its XML. This changes the result for every
   non-ASCII .xlsx: sheet names (the keys of the hash a workbook is read
   into), column names, row names and every string cell, shared or inline.
   A workbook write_table() wrote from the keys "café" and "αβ" used to
   read back with keys of 5 and 4 bytes, so $book->{"\x{3b1}\x{3b2}"}
   found nothing and a cell "α" was 2 bytes; it now round-trips. ASCII
   text is unchanged, and so is every delimited file. Code that decoded
   these strings itself must stop, or it decodes twice.
 - For an .xlsx, sheet, row_names, keep_cols, drop_cols, colClasses
   names, filter keys and na_strings tokens are compared as characters. A
   byte string that is valid UTF-8 is decoded first, so a name typed
   without `use utf8` still matches.
 - Text that is not valid UTF-8, which Excel and LibreOffice never write,
   is not an error: that string is returned as its bytes, without the
   UTF-8 flag, as every string was before.
 - A warning that names such a column or row (a keep_cols or drop_cols
   name that is no column, a repeated column or row name) gives the name
   in UTF-8 bytes, which is what perl prints for a string of characters;
   warn() of the characters themselves would warn "Wide character", which
   the module's fatal warnings make an error.

 [Behavior change: blank rows of an .xlsx]

 - read_table() now reads a row with no value that lies between an
   .xlsx's header and its last row with a value as a row of undef, as
   pandas' read_excel() reads it (GH 39808), where it dropped it. That
   holds for a row written empty, <row r="3"/> or <row r="3"></row> as
   write_table() writes a row of empty cells, for one holding only
   formatted empty cells, and for one missing from the XML, as Excel
   leaves an empty row out: a row's r= now says how many blank rows lie
   before it. A table write_table() wrote with a row of undef in it lost
   that row on the way back. Rows past the last value are still not
   read, as pandas does not read them (Excel records formatted rows
   below a table), and the header is still the first row with a value.
 - With output_type => 'hoh' a blank row is still left out: it has no
   row name, and an undefined one is refused, which would have made any
   sheet with a spacer row unreadable as a hash of hashes.

 [Behavior change: write_table() writes delimited text as UTF-8]

 - A field perl holds as bytes that are not valid UTF-8 is now read as
   Latin-1 and written as UTF-8, as the .xlsx and LaTeX writers already
   wrote it. "caf\xe9" and "café" are the same string to perl, but the
   first was written as the single byte E9, which Python's csv, pandas and
   R all read as "caf\x{FFFD}", and the second as C3 A9. Both are now
   written C3 A9. Text with the UTF-8 flag on, and bytes that are valid
   UTF-8, such as the fields read_table() returns from a UTF-8 file, are
   written as before, so reading a UTF-8 file and writing it back still
   gives the same bytes; a Latin-1 file read and written back comes out
   as UTF-8. Writing a 200000 x 20 table is about 2% slower.
 - A lone surrogate, which only broken data holds, is still written
   rather than refused: as perl's three bytes for it in a delimited file,
   and as _xD800_ in an .xlsx, which LibreOffice shows as an empty cell.
   README.md now says so, where it said LibreOffice decodes every escape.

 [write_table() to an .xlsx]

 - A string was written as a number cell, and so shown as another text,
   when it had a trailing 0 after the point (6.10, 1.0, 0.50), a point
   with no digit after it (1.) or none before it (.5), an exponent (1e5,
   2.5e-3) or a minus sign on zero (-0): Excel and LibreOffice showed 6.1,
   1, 0.5 and 100000, so section 6.10 of a document read as section 6.1.
   Such a string is now text, and the POD's "a number cell only when Excel
   would show it as it stands" holds. A value perl holds as a number is
   written as before. t/write_table.xlsx.number.python.t checks the sheet
   XML against what openpyxl 3.1.5 and LibreOffice 24.2.7.2 show.

 [Formulas]

 - Every function that reads a formula through lm_formula_terms() now
   expands a parenthesised group of terms as R's terms.formula() does:
   (a + b)*c, a*(b + c), (a + b):c, (a + b + c)^2, (a + b)/c, a %in% b,
   nested groups and - (a:b). These died with "cannot evaluate term"
   (until 0.3419, with "0 degrees of freedom"), so car's own vif()
   example, (income + education)*type, had to be written out.
 - Terms are ordered by degree and then by appearance, and an interaction
   is named in R's variable order, so y ~ x*z*w - x*z now labels its
   interactions x:w, z:w and x:z:w as R does, where it gave w:x, w:z and
   w:x:z.
 - A bare a/b is R's nesting, a + a:b; a ratio of two columns is I(a/b).
   Through 0.3425 a/b was read as the ratio. A column name containing %
   now croaks.
 - A power that is not a whole number from 2 to 64, an unbalanced
   parenthesis, an operator with no operand, a %op% other than %in% and
   an intercept marker inside a group are errors rather than guesses.
   Two departures from R remain, both in README: a lone term crossed with
   itself (wt*wt) keeps the product, and intercept markers are read only
   at the top level.
 - A factor is now coded by contrasts when its margin lies inside any
   earlier term, as R's TermCode() does, and not only when it equals one.
   y ~ A:U + A:V - 1 gave A:V dummy coding, the mistake the comment at R's
   tests/reg-tests-2.R line 707 says R 1.5.1 made.
 - t/formula_groups.R.t checks groups against R 4.6.1's term labels and
   coefficients through lm, glm, aov, anova, zerotrunc, hurdle, svyglm,
   ivreg, lmer, coxph and vif.

   GVIF per predictor together with the terms it interacts with, and the
   "Interacts With" and "Other Predictors" columns. It refuses what car

 [binom_test()]

   dbinom(i) over the far side of the mode wherever it is no larger than
   dbinom(x) * (1 + 1e-7), a loop of up to n steps, so binom_test(3,
   1e18) never returned (R itself tries to allocate 37 GB). The pmf is
   unimodal, so those indices are one run at the far end of the side, and

 - Stats::LikeR::Usage is no longer indexed. It holds the help screens
   printed above a calling error, has no POD and no interface of its own,
   and MetaCPAN listed it beside Stats::LikeR as a module with no abstract.

 [Documentation]

 - The Synopsis is now a runnable example: read a table, summarize it, take
   a mean and sd, compare two groups with t_test() and fit lm(). The prose
   that was there moves to a new Description, which now says where these
   functions follow R rather than List::Util: min(), max(), sum(), mean(),
   median(), sd() and var() croak when called with no arguments, where
   List::Util returns undef, and a NaN in the input makes the result NaN.

 - add_data()'s resulting structures are written as Perl data rather than
   JSON, and the mixed-hash example now shows the target it starts from.

 - age_standardize() documents an example value for se, 114.4. R gives the
   same value for the example's data from sqrt(sum(w^2 * count / pop^2)),
   with w the standard population's weights, scaled by per.

 [rank()]

 - ties_method => 'random' seeds the generator before drawing, as runif()
   and sample() do. It called Drand01() without AUTO_SEED_PRNG(), so a
   process that never called srand() drew from an unseeded generator, and
   every run broke ties in the same order.

 - A tied array, a tied element and a tied scalar argument are ranked by
   their values. Elements were tested with SvOK() before their get magic
   ran, so every element of a tied array read as undef: a tied (3, 1, 2)
   ranked as 1 2 3, the ranks of three NAs. Each is now fetched once.

 - An array that grows while it is read, through a FETCH that pushes onto
   it, is read only as far as it was counted. The gather loop took each
   array's length again, so a growing array could write past the end of
   the work buffers.

 - The work buffers are on the save stack, so a croak part-way through,
   from an overloaded value or a FETCH that dies, no longer leaks them.
   They were freed by hand at the end. t/rank.tied_random.t covers all
   four.

 [lm() and glm()]

 - A predictor is aliased by R's rule: when what the columns before it
   leave of it has a norm below 1e-7 of its own (lm.fit()'s tol), or
   min(1e-7, epsilon/1000) for glm(), as glm.fit() has it. The test was
   1e-10 on a squared pivot of X'X, which is 1e-5 on the norm, so a
   predictor such as x = 1e4 + noise of sd 0.05, which R fits, came back
   NaN from lm() and from gaussian and poisson glm() alike. vif() asks the
   same question and gets the same answer.

 - Both fit by factoring X, with AS 274 Givens rotations as anova() and
   aov() already did and one step of refinement on the residuals, rather
   than by solving the normal equations, which square the condition
   number. On R's longley data (kappa 2.4e7) the estimates were 2.7e-8
   from R's and are now within 3e-12; across t/lm.R.scipy.t's 42 designs
   the worst disagreement with R fell from 1.3e-8 to 6.9e-12.

 - lm() is 6 to 14 times faster on a wide design: 0.36 s, against 5.1 s,
   for y ~ x + g on 2e5 rows with 50 levels of g, and 0.46 s against 3.0
   s for 40 numeric columns. It built X'X with a column-strided walk for
   every pair of columns. glm()'s iterations do more work per row than
   X'X did, and the same poisson fit takes 0.97 s against 0.72 s.

 - t/lm.collinear.R.t has R's longley and PR#2776 cases, SciPy's
   test_regress_against_R data shifted by 1e7, and Wilkinson's NASTY
   regressions.

 [cor_test()]

 - continuity => 1 corrects Spearman's asymptotic t as R does, adding 1 to
   n(n^2 - 1)/6 before rho is formed from S, and takes the two-sided tail
   S lies in. It was ignored, with a warning that R ignores it too, which
   R does not: on R's own case, x = 1:5 against y = (8, 6, 7, 5, 3), R's
   two-sided p is 0.0969 and cor_test() gave the uncorrected 0.0374.
   t/cor_test.spearman_continuity.R.t crosses every case with both
   settings.

 [Values with get magic]

 - pt(), qt(), pchisq(), qchisq(), pf(), qf() and pbinom() read a capture
   variable or a tied scalar passed positionally: after "10" =~ /(\d+)/,
   pt(2.5, $1) croaked "'(undef)' was given with no value", because the
   argument was tested with SvOK() before its magic had run.

 - The same order made p_adjust() read a tied p-value in a flat list as
   undef, which it counts as 1; kruskal_test() drop a tied cell in either
   input form; friedman_test() drop a block with a tied cell; and aov()
   without a formula leave a tied cell out. t/tied_cell.magic_order.t
   covers each.

 [Tied cells that change the data being read]

 - A FETCH that frees, grows or empties the container being read no longer
   makes these read freed memory, which valgrind showed for each and which
   segfaulted or panicked several: median() of two arrays (a FETCH that
   grew the second wrote past the buffer; it now croaks), kruskal_test()'s
   x and g form (a FETCH that emptied g), hoa2aoh(), hoa2hoh(),
   add_data(), vals(), avals(), sample() of an array and of a hash,
   scale() of a matrix, and prcomp(). Each now holds the rows and columns
   it reads, or re-reads an array's block after every FETCH.
   t/tied_cell.free_mid_read.t covers each.

 - A FETCH that dies no longer leaks: cor()'s buffers (310 kB a call for
   two vectors of 20000, 145 kB for a 300 x 60 matrix), matrix()'s half-
   built result (20004 SVs for 2 x 10000), friedman_test()'s buffers,
   vals() and avals()'s copies, and sample()'s entry table for a hash.
   Each is on the save stack or mortal from the start.

 [Croaks that leaked or exited]

 - A formula crossing more than 16 terms with '*' croaks without leaking
   the term lists it had built, 0.66 kB a call, in lm(), glm() and every
   function that reads a formula through lm_formula_terms().

 - runif(), rnorm() and rbinom() croak on an n there is no memory for, as
   matrix() already did, and add_data() on a numeric key that would extend
   an array past it. runif(1e11) took the interpreter down with "Out of
   memory in perl:util:safesysmalloc", which eval cannot catch.

 [Distribution functions]

 - pt(), pf(), qt() and qf() on the log scale were wrong, or NaN, in the
   far tail when one shape of the incomplete beta was at least 1000 and the
   other at most 1, as at large df. incbeta_xy_core() sent such cases to
   bgrat(), whose expansion is poor for a tiny variable; it now chooses the
   method as R's bratio() does, which for a tiny variable is TOMS 708's
   power series, bpser(). Up to 0.3413 pt(-3000, 5000, log => 1) was NaN,
   pt(-960, 2508.3, log => 1) was -7415.88159 for -7415.88469, and
   qt(-7500, 2500, log => 1) was -1001.09374 for -1001.09067.
   t/pt.log_tail.R.t pins the four functions against R 4.6.1; in 14 rows
   R's own qt() and qf() are off, and those take mpmath's value at 60
   digits, solved by bisection.

 [Model frames]

 - lm(), glm(), anova(), aov() and the formula readers behind zerotrunc(),
   hurdle(), svyglm(), ivreg(), lmer(), coxph() and vif() took the data's
   shape and row count from whichever hash entry perl returned first, so
   the result depended on hash order. A row-name column that came first and
   was shorter or longer than the data made every data column fail the
   length check ("HoA columns have unequal lengths"), and a plain scalar
   entry such as note => 'meta' croaked "Hash values must be ArrayRefs"
   when it came first and was ignored otherwise. The shape is now decided
   from the whole hash and n from the data columns, and a scalar entry in a
   hash of arrays is always ignored, as assign() ignores it and as R's
   model.frame() ignores a variable the formula does not name.
   t/lm_read_rows.order.t runs each case under 24 hash seeds.

   pmax(exp(eta), .Machine$double.eps) for poisson and negbin, and for the
   logit R's logit_linkinv(), which clamps eta at +-30, with mu.eta a
   function of eta. The poisson and negbin mean and variance were floored
   at 1e-10 and the binomial mean at 10 * DBL_EPSILON, so a fit with fitted
   rates far below 1e-10 was off by up to 4e-10 in its coefficients (slope
   1.0734182285526 where R gives 1.0734182281786); it now agrees with R to
   rounding. t/glm_mu_floor.R.t has the cases, and t/model_pvalue_tails.t's
   huge-z binomial case moves with it.

   by packing their integer labels into one key, rather than building a
   Perl hash per intersection, in glm() and ivreg(). The partition, its
   numbering and every result are bit for bit unchanged; a poisson fit on
   1e6 rows with three cluster variables went from 3.25 s to 1.22 s, and
   with two from 1.64 s to 1.03 s.

 [Count models]

 - The digamma and trigamma behind glm(family => 'negbin')'s theta and
   zerotrunc() and hurdle() were good to only 2e-10 and 1.7e-8: the
   recurrence stopped at x = 6 and the series was cut after B_8. They now
   take a 12-term series from x = 7 (9 on long double, 50 on __float128)
   and agree with mpmath to a few ulp, and the standard error of theta
   agrees with R to 2.4e-13, where it was 6.7e-9 out. nb_theta_ml() also
   computes them once per Newton step rather than once per row.

 [lmer()]

 - The criterion no longer passes over all n rows each time the optimizer
   evaluates it: X'X, X'y and the least-squares residual terms are formed
   once per fit, so an evaluation costs only the per-block factorizations.
   A random-slope fit with 50 groups at n = 200,000 went from 2.5 s to 0.12
   s, a random intercept from 0.51 s to 0.09 s, and two grouping factors
   from 1.3 s to 0.19 s. The residual sum of squares is expanded about the
   least-squares fit rather than from y'y, so it does not cancel when y has
   a large mean, and the reported fit still takes an exact residual pass;
   theta, sigma and the coefficients agree with the previous code to about
   1e-9.

   rather than the double M_PI, which put a constant offset of about n *
   4e-17 into both on long-double and quadmath perls.

 [interpolate()]

 - A NaN cell is a gap, as pandas treats it, for every method and every
   limit, limit_direction and limit_area. Only undef was, and a NaN was
   taken for an anchor, so [1, undef, 3, NaN, 5, undef, 7, 8, 9]
   interpolated with method => 'cubic' came back 1 NaN 3 NaN 5 NaN 7 8 9
   where pandas gives 1 to 9, and under any method that fits the whole
   column one NaN made every gap NaN. A NaN in the x coordinates croaks, as
   pandas refuses a NaN index; it used to pass the increasing check, since
   every comparison with NaN is false. t/interpolate.nan.pandas.t pins
   about 1,700 cases against pandas 3.0.4 over the whole limit space.

 - limit is applied in O(n), not O(n * limit): each gap rescanned its whole
   window, so one 200,000-cell gap with limit_direction => 'both' took 4.1
   s at limit 100000 and now takes 0.03 s. The cells filled are unchanged
   on 12,000 random frames.

 [qcut()]

 - NaN is missing, as it is to pandas, as well as undef: it is left out of
   the cutpoints and its code comes back undef. A NaN was binned as a
   number, and every edge it touched came back NaN. t/qcut.nan.pandas.t has
   pandas' test_qcut_nas and test_qcut_nullable_integer cases.

 [p_adjust()]

 - Holm's running maximum started at 0, where R's cummax() has no floor,
   and hommel was clamped to 1, which R's is not, so p-values outside [0,
   1] came back differently from R: p_adjust([-1, 0.5, 2], 'holm') was 0 1
   1 for R's -3 1 1. Values in [0, 1] are unchanged.

 - The p-values are sorted with an inlined sort rather than qsort() and a
   comparator, with the same order: 1,000,000 of them take 0.11 s, against
   0.22 s.

 [rbinom()]

 - size is a trial count, bounded by what the generator can carry, IV_MAX
   of the running perl, rather than by the 2^48 meant for element counts:
   rbinom(n => 3, size => 1e15, prob => 0.3) draws, as R does, where it
   croaked "size is too large". On a perl with 32-bit integers a size
   between 2^31 and 2^32 croaks instead of running billions of Bernoulli
   trials.

 [predict()]

 - An interaction term was copied into a 512-byte buffer to find its factor
   components, so an interaction of long names lost the factor and every
   row came back NaN; it is scanned in place now. The unseen-level error no
   longer cuts the factor's name and level at 256 bytes.
   t/predict.long_names.t compares predict() with lm()'s fitted values for
   names up to 1200 bytes.

 [filter()]

 - A compiled predicate held borrowed pointers to every cell of a row while
   it tested them, so a tied cell whose FETCH cleared the row left the next
   test reading a freed scalar. A row with a tied cell now holds its cells
   for the test. t/tied_cell.filter_clears_row.t has the case; valgrind
   cannot show the old read, because perl frees scalars into its own
   arenas.

 [csort()]

 - A numeric column sorts about twice as fast, 0.21 s against 0.40 s for a
   million doubles: each cell is read once into a (value, row) pair and the
   pairs are sorted with an inlined comparison, ties broken by row, so the
   order is the one the stable merge sort gave, with undef, missing and NaN
   last in their original order.

 - Sorting an array of hashes into "hoa" or "aoa" no longer makes a mortal
   SV for every input cell: the key-union passes look each key up by its
   stored bytes and make an SV only for a new name, as merge() does. On
   200,000 rows of 22 columns the peak fell from +355 MB to +170 MB ("hoa")
   and from +377 MB to +192 MB ("aoa"), and the call is about 30% faster.
   The column names are ordered with qsort() rather than an insertion sort;
   two names with the same bytes, one UTF-8 and one not, are now ordered by
   that flag rather than by hash order.

 [oneway_test()]

 - The formula form made a mortal key for every row, which lived until the
   call returned: a million-row call peaked 71 MB above its baseline. One
   key is reused, and the peak is 24 MB.

 [write_table()]

 - An .xlsx is checksummed eight bytes at a time (slicing-by-8, byte loads
   only), so a 100000 x 20 mixed table, 101 MB, writes in 0.5 s rather than
   0.7 s, byte for byte the same file.

 [Portability]

 - LikeR.xs uses NV_NAN and NV_INF throughout in place of the C99 NAN and
   INFINITY, and formats row numbers with perl's UVuf rather than a C
   "%lu", which is 32 bits wide on Windows.

   that is not a number, but `looks_like_number()` accepts `NaN`, and `NaN`
   fails no comparison: it passed the `t < 0` check, and in the risk-set loop
   `o[j].time == t` never held. `survfit([1, 'nan', 3], [1, 1, 1])` pushed
   onto its curve until the kernel killed perl for running out of memory, and
   `logrank_test` with the same time never returned. Both now croak "time at
   index 1 is NaN". A `NaN` status, which used to read as an event, croaks
   the same way.

   censored, or 2 = event and 1 = censored when the largest value is 2.
   `survfit` and `logrank_test` used to take any nonzero status as an event,
   so a 1/2-coded column, such as R's own `lung` data, made every row a
   death: `logrank_test` on status `(2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2)` gave chi-squared 5.05

   0 was present; `Surv()` calls such a 0 invalid. All three share one reader

   a warning.

   to `looks_like_number()`, so all three used to croak "status at index 1
   is not a number" on the result of a comparison, which `Surv()` takes as
   `FALSE`.

   does. It used to be read as "", so it made a group of its own named "" and
   was pooled with any row whose label really was "".

   is weighted by S(t-)^rho, the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate just before it,
   and `rho => 1` is Peto & Peto's modification of the Gehan-Wilcoxon test.
   Nothing after the third argument used to be read, so `rho => 1` was
   accepted and answered as the log-rank test. `observed` and `expected` are

 [pchisq(), qchisq() and every chi-square p-value]

 - The incomplete gamma lost all accuracy at a large df. It was Numerical
   Recipes' series and continued fraction times exp(-x + a log x -
   lgamma(a)), whose exponent is a difference of numbers near a log a, and
   the series stopped on an absolute 1e-15 term. pchisq(1e15, 1e15) was 0.379
   where R gives 0.50000000594708038, and pchisq(1e10, 1e10) was 0.4999978
   for 0.5000019. It is R's own pgamma.c now (Morten Welinder's algorithm: a
   saddle-point Poisson prefactor, relative stopping rules, and Temme's
   expansion near the median), computed in NV arithmetic. Its series
   constants are double precision, as R's are, so a long-double or quadmath
   perl now gets about double's accuracy from it rather than its own. The
   same routine is behind chisq_test, cmh_test, coxph, friedman_test, ivreg,
   kruskal_test, logrank_test, mcnemar_test, prop_test and age_standardize.

 - log => 1 on pchisq() is carried through the series, as in R, rather than
   being log() of the probability: a tail a hair under 1 logs to the tiny
   negative number it is, where it used to log to exactly 0.

 [pt(), pf(), pbinom() and the incomplete beta at a large shape]

   formed log(b/(a + b)) as log1p(-a/(a + b)), so pt(1.96, df = 1e15) was
   0.97448286722801003 for R's 0.97500210485177941 and qt(0.975, 1e15) was
   1.974 for 1.95996; and its continued fraction loses about max(a, b) eps
   relative, so pf(1, 1e15, 1e15) was 0.481 where F and 1/F share a
   distribution and the answer is exactly 0.5. From a shape of 1000 up it
   takes TOMS 708's algorithms now, as R's pbeta() does: bfrac(), basym()
   near the mean of two large shapes, and bgrat() when the smaller shape is
   at most 1. Below 1000 nothing changed but the front factor, which is TOMS
   708's brcomp() form. This is behind t_test, cor_test, anova, lm,
   oneway_test, var_test and binom_test too.

   0.5 is R's 2.9643938750474793e-323 rather than 0. The test pinned 0 as a
   deliberate divergence; it was the incomplete beta losing the far tail of
   P(X >= n - y), which the new one computes as R does.

   R's limits now: pt is pnorm, pf(x, df1, Inf) is pchisq(x df1, df1), pf(x,
   Inf, df2) is the upper pchisq(df2/x, df2), and with both infinite F is a
   step at 1, with 0.5 at 1 itself; qt and qf invert them, and qt takes the
   normal quantile from df > 1e20, as R does. Perl's 9**9**9 and the string

   group used to scan every row twice, which was O(groups x rows): 200,000
   rows in 5,000 groups took 1.15 s and take 0.14 s now. Two groups cost
   what they did.

   skips groups with nobody left at risk, and no longer allocates a buffer at

   it was.

   whichever tail it was given. It bisected, against an incomplete gamma that

   ms a call and takes 2.2 us, and qchisq(0.5, 1e15) took 0.26 s and takes

 [usage]

 [df2h(), which was aoh2h()]

 - aoh2h() is now df2h(), and folds two columns of any of the four data
   frame shapes into a plain hash, where it took an array of hashes alone.
   An AoA's columns are integer positions, defaulting to 0 and 1, which is
   what tibble's deframe() reads; a negative position counts back from the
   end of each row, as $row->[-1] does. A HoA's two columns must be the
   same length, and row i is element i of each. A HoH's row names are not
   used.

   concat. Every AoH it took before folds the same way, but its messages
   now begin "df2h:" rather than "aoh2h:". A hash it used to refuse as
   "not an arrayref of hashrefs" is now read as a HoA or HoH, and a flat
   hash, the likely mistake, gets a message of its own. h('aoh2h') shows
   df2h's documentation.

   have no order and either would keep a different row from run to run.
   When a HoH has more than one bad row, the message names the first in

   sort, and are read again sorted only once that has croaked, so a frame
   that folds pays nothing for this.

   still FETCHed once. The AoH fold is the 0.3218 XS code unchanged, and
   keeps its speed and memory figures.
