 [`read_table`]

 - Bug fixes:

 - **A comment-prefixed header is now read correctly.** `read_table` strips a
     leading comment marker from the header line (so a file may begin with
     `#id,val`), but that strip was dead code: the XS parser skipped *every* line
     beginning with the comment string before the callback ever saw it, so a
     commented header was silently dropped and the first data row was mistaken for
     the header. The parser now delivers the first content line even when it
     begins with the comment marker, and only skips comment lines after the header
     has been seen.

 - **Carriage returns inside quoted fields are preserved.** The parser stripped
     `\r` unconditionally, so a quoted value such as `"x\ry"` lost its carriage
     return and would not survive a `write_table` -> `read_table` round-trip. `\r`
     is now stripped only as part of a trailing CRLF line ending and as a stray CR
     *outside* quotes; inside quotes it is literal data.

 - **Duplicate column names no longer corrupt `hoa` output.** With
     `output.type => 'hoa'`, a repeated column name pushed the same cell once per
     occurrence, so the affected columns came out longer than the others and the
     arrays no longer lined up by row. Columns are now keyed by unique header name
     (first-seen order preserved, later values win, one warning emitted).

 - **A defined non-CODE callback is now an error.** Passing a defined argument
     that was not a CODE reference silently fell through to slurp mode and ignored
     the argument; it now croaks
     (*"callback must be a CODE reference"*).

 - **An undefined/empty `hoh` row-name now dies instead of keying on `""`.**
     With `output.type => 'hoh'`, a row whose row-name column was empty/undef was
     stored under the `''` key and raised *"uninitialized value"* warnings. It now
     dies, naming the column and the offending data row.

 - **A numeric filter key past the last column now dies.** A 1-based numeric
     filter key greater than the column count was accepted, then silently extended
     every row through the `$_` write-back. It is now rejected up front with a
     message naming the column count.

 - **`sep` and `delim` together now die.** Supplying both silently preferred
     `delim`; passing both is now an explicit error (`delim` remains an alias for
     `sep` when used alone).

 - **The library no longer prints to STDOUT.** The unknown-argument path used
     `say` to dump the offending names to STDOUT before dying; the names are now
     carried in the `die` message itself.

 - Better diagnostics:

 - Alignment errors now report **which data row** is ragged
     (*"Alignment error on FILE data row N (X fields vs Y headers)"*), instead of
     only the field/header counts.

 - Memory-leak fixes (exception paths):

 - The parser allocated its working buffers (`current_row`, `field`, and — in
   slurp mode — `data`) in the XS `INIT:` block, i.e. *before* any validation, and
   freed them only by falling off the end of the function. Any non-local exit
   therefore leaked:

 - the open-failure `croak` leaked the row buffer and field (and the slurp
     accumulator);
 - far more commonly, a `die` thrown **inside the row callback** — which
     `read_table` does routinely on alignment errors, bad row names, and filter
     exceptions — unwound straight out of the XS frame and leaked the field, the
     current row, the line buffer, the slurp accumulator, *and the open file
     handle*.

 - Allocations now happen in `CODE:` after every croak-able check, and every
   long-lived resource (the file handle via `SAVEDESTRUCTOR_X`, the buffers via
   `SAVEFREESV`) is tied to the save stack, which an exception unwinds. Measured
   with `Test::LeakTrace`: a `die` mid-file went from 5 leaked SVs to 0, and an
   open failure from 2 to 0. This is the likely source of the constant-size leaks
   seen in CPAN-tester reports for the exception-path tests.

 - Performance:

 - **~2.5x faster parsing** (57 -> 145 MB/s on a 100k-row quoted file). The core
     loop appended one character at a time with `sv_catpvn(field, &ch, 1)`; it now
     scans runs of ordinary bytes with `memchr` / a bounded scan and appends each
     run in a single `sv_catpvn`, copying field contents in bulk rather than byte
     by byte.

 - Internal / non-behavioral:

 - XS declarations moved from `INIT:` to `PREINIT:`; allocations deferred into
     `CODE:` (see the leak fixes above).
 - The filter loop now aliases the row hash with `local *_ = \%line_hash`
     instead of copying it with `local %_ = %line_hash`. This removes a full
     per-row hash copy for every filtered row and fixes a latent staleness bug:
     after a filter mutated `$_` and the change was written back, `%_` still
     reflected the pre-mutation copy, so a subsequent filter in the same row saw
     stale values. With aliasing, `%_` *is* the row, so write-backs are always
     visible.

 - Known limitation (not changed):

 - **`undef.val` does not round-trip back to `undef`.** `write_table` renders an
     `undef` cell as an empty field by default, and `read_table` maps an empty
     field back to `undef`, so the *default* round-trip is clean. But if a file is
     written with a token such as `'undef.val' => 'NA'`, `read_table` has no
     inverse option and reads `NA` back as the string `'NA'`. `read_table` also
     cannot distinguish a deliberately quoted empty string (`""`) from a missing
     value -- both become `undef`. Adding an `na.strings`-style option to
     `read_table` (mapping configurable tokens and/or empty fields to `undef`)
     would close this gap.

 [`write_table`]

 - Behavior change:

 - **`undef` cells now write as an empty field, not an empty string.** A missing
     or `undef` value renders as nothing between separators (`a,,c`) rather than a
     quoted empty string (`a,'',c` / `a,"",c`). Supplying `'undef.val' => 'NA'`
     (or any other token) still overrides this, exactly as before. This is the
     only change that can alter the bytes of an existing output file; if you relied
     on the previous default, pass `'undef.val' => ''` to keep an explicit empty
     field, or your chosen placeholder.

 - Bug fixes:

 - **Wide-character / UTF-8 column names and row keys now round-trip.**
     Previously, cells were looked up with the raw bytes of the column name
     (`hv_fetch(..., SvPV_nolen(name), strlen(name), ...)`), which fails to match a
     UTF-8-flagged hash key: the column header printed correctly but every cell
     under it came back empty. All lookups now fetch by SV (`hv_fetch_ent`), header
     lists are gathered and sorted as SVs (`sortsv` + `sv_cmp`, preserving the
     flag) instead of being round-tripped through `char *`, and the `row.names`
     column is matched with `sv_eq` rather than `strcmp`. Embedded NUL bytes in
     keys are handled correctly as a side effect.

 - **`col.names => []` no longer loops forever.** An empty `col.names` array made
     `av_len()` return `-1`, which — compared against an unsigned `size_t` loop
     index — wrapped to `SIZE_MAX` and ran effectively without end. This was fixed
     for flat hashes previously; it was still present for hash-of-hashes,
     hash-of-arrays, and array-of-hashes, plus both `row.names` header-filtering
     loops. All such loops now use a signed index.

 - **Tables wider than 65,535 columns no longer hang.** One header loop used an
     `unsigned short` index that silently wrapped past 65,535 and never terminated.
     It now uses `size_t` like the rest of the code.

 - **Flat-hash cells holding a reference now croak.** Every other input shape
     rejects a nested reference with
     *"Cannot write nested reference types to table"*; a flat hash instead
     stringified it (e.g. `ARRAY(0x55...)`) into the file. It now croaks
     consistently.

 - **`'undef.val' => undef` is handled cleanly.** It previously called
     `SvPV_nolen` on `undef`, raising an *"uninitialized value"* warning and
     yielding an empty string by accident. It is now treated explicitly as an empty
     field, with no warning.

 - Memory-leak fixes (exception paths):

 - The row-key list gathered for hash-of-hashes input was leaked when the output
     file could not be opened.
 - The *"Could not get headers"* croak on hash-of-arrays input leaked both the

 - Numeric row labels are now formatted into a reused stack buffer instead of a

     cast-away-`const` and one allocation per row).
 - Several signed/unsigned index types were made consistent (`SSize_t` vs

   bpser() (59 epsilons of a __float128 at I_0.8(15/2, 1/1024)) or the
   fraction; where R uses apser() or fpser() it took bpser(), whose
   answer is 1 minus a near-1 tail: 5.8e31 epsilons of a __float128 at a
   shape of 2^-130, and 1.9e17 of a long double at 2^-70.
 - basym() formed 2/3 as a double, which left I_x(3e11, 1e12) 1e-23 off
   on a __float128 (3.5e12 of its epsilons) wherever the two shapes were
   unequal and past 1e5. The asymptotic coefficients of digamma() and
   trigamma() were double quotients too, 3e-22 off on a __float128;
   digamma feeds apser(), glm()'s negative binomial theta and
   zerotrunc().
 - Against mpmath at 110 digits, counted as 0.3426 counts, the worst
   error is now 4 epsilons of a __float128 and 3 of a long double for
   the gamma (47 and 18 on the same cases before) and 10 and 11 for the
   beta (3.5e12 and 1.9e17), shapes from 2^-130 to 1e15. A double perl
   is unchanged, to the last bit over 81234 values.
 - On a __float128 perl qt() is up to twice as slow where its pt() calls
   take bup() and bgrat() (qt(0.975, 12): 1.0 ms, was 0.53 ms), and a
   continued fraction about 1.3 times; on a long double, 1.8 and 1.1.
 - t/incomplete.gamma.beta.mpmath.t has 239 more cases, 861 tests in
   all: gamma shapes 1e11 to 1e15 (Temme's expansion) and beta shapes to
   1e15, whose references are mpmath's integral of the density, checked
   against the series and fractions where both reach (they agree to
   1e-101); a < 1 with x from 1 to 3; the region of bup() and bgrat();
   and shapes of 2^-70 and 2^-130, which a double build skips. Its
   tolerances are tightened to the new errors (the long double's gamma
   from 32 to 8 units, the __float128's from 144 to 16).

 [pnorm() and qnorm() on long-double and __float128 perls]

 - pnorm() was R's double-precision port of Cody's algorithm on every
   build, so on a long-double or __float128 perl it agreed with the truth
   to about 1e-16 however wide the NV, and was 0 below z = -38.47, R's
   cut-off for a double, although such an NV holds the tail down to
   z = -150. On an x87 long double or a __float128 perl with the matching
   libm (the builds whose incomplete gamma and beta 0.3426 widened) it now
   computes from that NV's erfc(), with the far tail taken from erfcx()
   so that nothing underflows before the answer does, and forms
   (x - mean) / sd at the NV's width. pnorm(-40) is 3.655893540915e-350
   there, where it was 0. pt() with df = Inf, which is pnorm(), follows.
 - qnorm() used a double literal for 1/sqrt(2 pi) in its series near the
   median, which put that literal's 1e-17 error into every quantile from
   p = 0.2 to 0.8 (qnorm(0.25) was 3e17 epsilons of a __float128 out); it
   now takes that constant at the NV's width. Its tail stopped after four
   Newton passes on the linear scale, not enough from Moro's start below
   p = 1e-200 at a __float128's width, and below p = 1e-300 it polished
   against the double pnorm() and stopped polishing altogether past
   log p = -1.3e9. On those builds every lower-tail quantile is now
   finished by Newton on log Phi(z) = log p at the NV's width, with the
   Mills ratio Phi/phi taken from erfcx() rather than as the exp() of a
   difference of two large logs, which is what limited R's polish. The
   same quantile serves every confidence interval and critical value in
   the module, so those gain the digits too.
 - Against mpmath at 110 digits, over 85 z from 0 to 1e150 (both tails and
   their logs) and 100 quantiles (p from 2^-1074 to 1 - 2^-53, log p to
   -1e100), the worst error, in t/incomplete.gamma.beta.mpmath.t's units,
   is now 1.3 epsilons of a long double and 1.1 of a __float128 for
   pnorm() (it was 1.2e16 and 7e30), and 2 for qnorm() on both (2.3e4 and
   1.3e19). t/pnorm.qnorm.mpmath.t pins those cases, with its generator
   t/pnorm.qnorm.mpmath.py. A double perl is unchanged, and so is the
   cut-off at z = -38.47 of the p-values the tests in the module report
   (approx_pnorm()), which keeps those the same on every build, as R's.
 - t/pnorm.t checked that pnorm(-40) is 0, which is true only of a double;
   it now checks pnorm(-200), which underflows on every NV.

0.3428 2026-11-22 CST 

 [Behavior change: rank() of strings]

 - rank() read every value with SvNV(), so rank("b", "a", "b") returned
   2, 2, 2 (each string was 0) with only "isn't numeric" warnings, "0x10"
   ranked as 0, and rank("abc", 5, 1) gave 1, 3, 2. It now follows R: when
   every non-missing value looks like a number (looks_like_number, so
   "1e1", " 3 " and "Inf" do) the ranking is numeric as before; when one
   does not, all the values are ranked as strings, so rank("b", "a", "b")
   is 2.5, 1, 2.5 and rank("abc", 5, 1) is 3, 2, 1, as R's
   rank(c("abc", 5, 1)). Every ties_method and na_last mode works in both
   ways. Strings are compared by codepoint, never by locale; R uses the
   locale's collation, so non-ASCII text may order differently.
 - A reference that is not an object overloading its numeric value (a
   hashref, a nested arrayref, a coderef) is now an error, as ranking a
   list is in R (reg-tests-1a.R:3266). It used to be ranked by address.
 - NaN stays NA in both modes.

 [Behavior change: numeric options that are not numbers]

 - t_test(x, mu => "abc") warned and ran as mu = 0; conf_level => "abc"
   ran as a level of 0. R stops. A numeric option or positional argument
   that is not a number now croaks "<name> is not a number" in t_test,
   wilcox_test (mu, conf_level, digits_rank, tol_root, edgeworth),
   var_test (ratio, conf_level), cor_test, prop_test, fisher_test,
   cmh_test, roc, survfit, epi_2x2, glm, zerotrunc, hurdle, svyglm, ivreg,
   lmer and coxph (conf_level, theta, epsilon, eps, maxit), binom_test (p,
   conf_level), density (adjust, n, cut, ext, from, to), bw_sj and bw_ucv
   (lower, upper, tol), power_t_test (n, delta, power, sd, sig_level,
   tol), bedroc and auroc (alpha, cutoff, fraction, active_frac),
   logrank_test (rho), prcomp (tol, rank), write_table (xlsx_freeze_rows,
   xlsx_freeze_cols), pnorm, dnorm, qnorm, pt, qt, pchisq, qchisq, pf, qf,
   pbinom (x, every parameter, mean, sd), ptukey and qtukey (every
   argument, nranges), seq (from, to, by), and, in Perl, age_standardize
   (conf_level, per) and table_one (digits, pct_digits). pt(1.5, dff =>
   5), whose misspelled name used to be read as df = 0, now croaks too.
   Numeric strings with surrounding space, "Inf", "NaN" and objects
   overloading their numeric value are still numbers, and an undef x is
   still NaN.
 - Not changed: scale's center and scale (which take words as well as
   numbers), and data vectors, where a string that is not a number is a
   missing value by design.

 [Behavior change: formula parser]

 - lm() now takes offset() terms, as R's lm does. It fits the response less
   the offset; fitted_values include the offset, residuals are the response
   less the fitted values, and r_squared and the F statistic are
   summary.lm()'s, which take the offset out of the fitted values first.
   The expressions come back in offset_terms, and predict() adds them, as
   R's predict.lm() and predict.glm() do. Through 0.3427 lm(y ~ x +
   offset(z)) croaked "cannot evaluate term".
 - offset() is read wherever a term may stand, as terms() does, not only at
   the start or after a `+`. It is a variable of the formula's algebra: a
   term that holds it is dropped (`cnt ~ x + offset(z)*a` is x and a), and
   `cnt ~ x - offset(z)` still has the offset. Each distinct offset() counts
   once, where `offset(z) + offset(z)` used to add it twice. An offset
   expression with a bare operator (`offset(u/2)`, `offset(-z)`,
   `offset(u+z)`, `offset(u-z)`) is evaluated as arithmetic; it used to be
   looked up as a column of that name, and every row dropped. glm(), anova(),
   aov(), zerotrunc(), hurdle(), svyglm() and coxph() read it the same way.
 - `.` leaves out every variable the response mentions, as R's CheckRHS()
   does: `log(y) ~ .` omits y, `I(y + x) ~ .` omits y and x, and
   `log(y) ~ . - x` leaves the rest. It used to omit only a column equal to
   the whole response text, so `log(y) ~ .` regressed log(y) on y.
 - The intercept markers act in order and the last wins, as in R: `y ~ x - 1
   + 1`, `y ~ 0 + x + 1` and `y ~ x + 0 + 1` now have an intercept, where the
   later `+ 1` used to be dropped silently.

 [Behavior change: a one-level factor is an error]

 - A categorical column with a single level in the model now stops the fit
   with R's message, "contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or
   more levels" (R 4.6.1 gives it for `y ~ one`, `y ~ one - 1` and
   `y ~ a:one` alike). lm(), glm(), aov(), anova() and the model-frame
   fitters used to drop the column silently and fit the model without the
   variable. aov()'s stacked form, whose one group is the caller's own
   factor, still fits it.
 - A factor's levels are now those of the rows the fit keeps, as in R's
   model.frame(drop.unused.levels = TRUE). A level that occurs only in
   rows dropped for a missing value in any variable of the model -- the
   response, an offset() term, offset => or weights => included -- used to
   stay a level, with a column of zeros whose coefficient came back NaN
   and an entry in xlevels. `lm('y~a+x')` with a level p held only by a
   row with an undef x now gives the Intercept, ar and x that R gives,
   and xlevels q r. Covers lm, glm, aov, anova, svyglm, ivreg, lmer,
   zerotrunc, hurdle, coxph and vif. Left open: with two formulas over
   the same rows (hurdle, ivreg, lmer's random parts) a row dropped only
   by the other formula's variables still counts.

 [Behavior change: read_table() of a damaged .xlsx]

 - A file that is not a zip archive, an archive cut short, and a member
   that is damaged now die with a message naming the file, as pandas
   raises zipfile.BadZipFile. A text file named junk.xlsx used to read as
   [], a truncated archive as no rows, and 8 corrupted bytes in deflate
   data as 1642 of 2000 rows, silently. The fallback reader no longer
   takes a non-archive for a member (Transparent => 0) and no longer
   reads a failed read as end of file.
 - The CRC-32 of every member is checked, as Python's zipfile checks it.
   It costs 3.7% of a read of a real 7.8 MB workbook (0.0132 s of 0.359 s)
   and 6.9% of a 197 MB worksheet of inline strings (0.0725 s of 1.05 s),
   using the writer's slice-by-8 CRC, which is faster than
   Compress::Raw::Zlib's.
 - A member whose size the central directory gives wrongly is an error
   instead of being inflated a second time by the fallback: a 537 MB
   member took 2.2 s and 1.07 GB, and now dies after 0.36 s.
 - Chart sheets, dialog sheets and macro sheets are no longer read as
   empty tables and counted as sheets, so a workbook of one worksheet and
   one chart sheet reads as that table, not a hash. A workbook with none
   but those dies.
 - Two sheets of one name die instead of the later replacing the earlier.

 [Behavior change: write_table()]

 - A write that dies partway no longer destroys an existing file or leaves
   a partial one. Output goes to a temporary file in the same directory,
   renamed over the name when the table is complete and removed on any
   croak, a tied FETCH's included, for .xlsx, delimited (compressed too)
   and LaTeX. The permission bits of a replaced file are kept; a hard
   link to it no longer shares the new contents. A name that is not a
   regular file (pipe, FIFO, /dev/null, a symlink) is written in place as
   before, and so is a file in a directory that cannot be written to. A
   compressed or LaTeX write that croaked used to leave a truncated file;
   it leaves nothing now.
 - An .xlsx wider than 16384 columns is refused before the file is opened
   when the shape fixes the width (a hash of arrays, col_names).
 - The LaTeX writer now applies the rule the other formats follow: valid
   UTF-8 as it stands, else read as Latin-1 and encoded. Headers, row
   names, cells and undef_val were written as the single byte E9 for
   "caf\xe9" beside C3 A9 for the same text flagged. tex_comment and
   tex_longtable_head are unchanged.

 [Behavior change: power_t_test()]

 - n below 2 is accepted, as R accepts it: power.t.test() takes the degrees
   of freedom as pmax(1e-7, n - 1) * tsample, so the t distribution is
   defined there. power_t_test(n => 1.5, delta => 1) is 0.0608734 as R's,
   and the power is exactly 0 from n = 1.001 down, where the critical value
   is infinite (R's qt() is Inf and its pt(Inf) is 0). It used to croak
   "'n' must be at least 2"; only n <= 0 does now.
 - Solving for n no longer croaks "no 'n' in [2, 1e+07]" when the target is
   already exceeded at n = 2: the root is looked for in (1, 2), as R's
   uniroot(extendInt = "upX") looks below 2. power => 0.2, delta => 5 is
   1.40673, as R's. For power => 0.01, delta => 0.1 R answers 1.07783,
   which is not the root: R's pt(ncp =) jumps at df ~ 0.16 (power 0.00163
   at n = 1.07784, 0.0275 at n = 1.0779) and uniroot stops on the jump.
   This returns 1.00244, where the continuous power reaches 0.01; the power
   at n = 1.05, 0.0265484548, agrees with mpmath, and R's is 0.00155.

 [Behavior change: epi_2x2()]

 - An exposure group with no subjects ([[0,0],[5,5]]) has no risk, so the
   odds ratio, risk ratio, risk difference, their intervals, nnt and that
   group's risk are NaN. The automatic +0.5 used to make them a risk ratio
   and odds ratio of exactly 1. epitools' riskratio() and oddsratio() give
   NaN (0/0). The +0.5 for a zero cell in a non-empty group is unchanged.

 [Bug fixes: formulas and design matrices]

 - A long sum no longer croaks "expands to too many terms" at about 2,900
   terms. Each `+` rebuilt the whole list and charged it, and the parse was
   O(k**2); a sum is now built in one accumulator, linear in its terms, and
   y ~ v1 + ... + v8000 parses in a fraction of a second.
 - A formula of a hundred thousand unary minus signs no longer overflows the
   C stack and kills the process; the signs are read in a loop.
 - A trailing operator (`y ~ x +`, `y ~ x + z +`, `y ~ +`, `y ~ 1 +`) croaks
   "the formula has an operator with no operand", as the 0.3426 notes say; a
   cleanup meant for the `+` an intercept marker leaves behind had been
   deleting it. `y ~ x z` and `y ~ x, z` were read as the one name `xz` after
   whitespace was stripped, and are now syntax errors.
 - Comparison and logic characters inside I() (`I(x > 0)`, `I(x == 0)`,
   `I(a == "a")`, `I(x & z)`, `I(x %% 2)`, `I(!x)`) croak "cannot evaluate
   term". R makes them logical factors, which this does not code; they used
   to report "0 degrees of freedom".
 - A column the data lack, in the response, a term, a function's argument or
   an offset, croaks "object 'q' not found", as R's does, naming the column,
   instead of "0 degrees of freedom". An unbalanced offset( reports
   "unbalanced parentheses in offset()" as before.
 - Without an intercept the factor coded by indicators for every level
   is now the one R picks: the first factor of two or more levels in the
   first term that has one (model.c, modelmatrix()). Before, a factor
   counted as full only when its margin was empty, so `y ~ x + b:x - 1`,
   `y ~ x/a - 1`, `y ~ x + z + b:x - 1`, `y ~ x + (x2:z/a) - 1` and
   `y ~ x + a:b - 1` fitted different columns from R's (x, x:bu and x:bv,
   the last aliased, for the first). The margin rule is R's TermCode(),
   whose empty margin is present with or without an intercept.
 - A factor crossed with itself is the factor, as in R: `a*a`, `a:a`,
   `c + c*c` and `(a + b)^3` with a repeated factor gave all-NaN product
   columns; they now give `a`. A term that becomes equal to an earlier
   one is dropped. A numeric variable's repeat is unchanged (`wt:wt` is
   `wt` squared, as the README says).
 - Coefficient, term, level and group_stats names are perl characters
   when the data are: a column found through its UTF-8 spelling, or a
   cell with the UTF-8 flag. With `use utf8` and a column "café",
   $fit->{coefficients}{"café"} now exists, and a level "ж" is no longer
   named `gÐ¶`. This covers coefficients, terms, xlevels, vcov, summary,
   confidence intervals, anova and aov row names, vif and the
   model-frame fitters. A script without `use utf8` gets the same bytes
   as before.
 - A design too wide to fit is refused, before anything large is
   allocated, with "design too wide (more than N columns ...)". X'X
   and the packed factor were allocated at p*p and p(p-1)/2 before the
   degrees of freedom were looked at, so `(v1+...+v30)^4` on 50 rows,
   32 640 columns, was killed for memory. The limit is 2 GiB for the two,
   about 13 000 columns for a double and 9 400 for a long double or
   __float128; R fits such models with NA coefficients, so this is a
   difference, now in the README.

 [Bug fixes: predict()]

 - predict() no longer croaks "newdata is missing column 'log(x)'" for a
   function of a numeric crossed with a factor (`y ~ g*log(x)`,
   `exp(x):a`, `sqrt(u):a`): only plain column names are looked up, and a
   call is evaluated. A factor level holding a ':' (the level "q:r")
   no longer makes every interaction predict NaN; the coefficient name
   is split at the ':' that separates components, not at every one.

 [Bug fixes: key encoding]

 - A key perl stored downgraded to Latin-1 (a `use utf8` literal such as "é"
   is stored as the byte E9, flagged WASUTF8) lost its UTF-8 flag wherever
   the XS copied it through HePV()/HeUTF8(), so it came back as the lone
   byte E9 where `keys %h` gives the character. Now fixed in colnames() and
   everything built on it (melt's `variable` column, the keys fillna() and
   bfill() add to the rows of a hash of hashes, summary()'s labels, which
   printed a bare E9, and table_one()'s), the outer keys of select_cols,
   drop_cols and rename_cols on a hash of hashes, the columns drop_cols and
   rename_cols keep, both levels of transpose(), p_adjust(), filter() on a
   hash of hashes, and kruskal_test()'s group_stats.

 [Bug fixes: frames]

 - dropna($hoa, rows => [...]) autovivified an undef column in the caller's
   frame, and dropna($hoa, cols => []) died "Can't use an undefined value as
   an ARRAY reference" on one; a non-array column died "Can't use string".
   Both now behave as cols => ['a'] does: an undef column is all undef, the
   frame is untouched, and a non-array column dies naming it.
 - melt() of an AoA with string column ids read them with SvIV() and left an
   IV on the caller's own SV, so the variable cells came out POK|IOK
   dualvars where 0.3424 gave plain strings. The id is read from a copy.
 - interpolate(): 'linear' now spaces the rows equally whatever `x` says, as
   the README says and pandas' linear ignores the index (index, values and
   time still use it); barycentric and krogh with a single numeric anchor
   fill the gap with that constant, as pandas does; quadratic and cubic on a
   column with no gap are returned as they are instead of dying "needs at
   least N numeric anchors"; and spline/polynomial with an order outside the
   IV range (1e30, inf) report the order given, not "got -1".
 - summary() counted a NaN as a value and returned NaN for every statistic.
   A NaN is now R's NA: left out of the statistics and counted in a
   trailing "NA's" column that appears when a variable has one.
   summary([1,'NaN',3,'Inf']) gives 3 values, Min 1, Median 3, Mean Inf,
   NA's 1, as R's summary() does.

 [Bug fixes: binom_test()]

 - An integer count is read exactly. A count held as an IV or UV, or a
   string spelling an integer, no longer goes through an NV, so on a double
   perl binom_test(4503599627370497, 9007199254740991, alternative =>
   'less') answers (R does) instead of croaking "x must be a nonnegative
   integer": v + 0.5 rounds to even from 2**52. binom_test(9007199254740993,
   9007199254740993) returned a statistic and parameter of
   9007199254740992 and 499999999999999000 came back as 499999999999998976,
   against the documented promise that counts are returned exactly up
   to IV_MAX; both are exact now. A non-integer number is still rounded
   to within 1e-7, without the +0.5.
 - binom_test(3, 9223372036854775806) croaked "n is too large (the limit
   is 9223372036854775806)" on a double perl, because (NV)IV_MAX rounds to
   2**63. The limit stated and the limit tested are now the same.
 - dbinom(), pbinom(), qbinom(), rbinom(), fisher_test(), mcnemar_test() and
   prop_test() were checked for the same flaw. They take their counts as NVs
   by R's design and return NVs, so there is nothing to lose; fisher_test()
   refuses cells above R's 2**31 - 1.

 [Bug fixes: density()]

 - n is rounded up, as R's seq.int(length.out = n) rounds it: n => 1.5 gives
   2 points, 2.5 gives 3, and 0.5 gives 1 where it croaked. It was read with
   SvIV(), which truncated, and on a perl with 32-bit integers n => 2**31
   and 2**32 wrapped into "'n' must be at least 1" instead of "'n' is too
   large".

 [Accuracy]

 - The incomplete beta behind pbinom(), pt(), pf() and qf() formed lambda
   = (a + b) y - b with a rounded product, which cost sqrt(n) epsilon at
   shapes of 1e13: pbinom(1765184560411, 17785315992617,
   7151671909757000 * 2**-56, lower = FALSE) was 0.0111407611194407633 on
   a long double perl for 0.0111407611194404998 (2.4e-14 relative). It is
   now a fused multiply-add (nv_fma, fmal in the long-double link probe in
   dist.ini and Makefile.PL) with the rounding error of a + b taken out,
   and the result is 5e-18 off. A long-double libm without fmal keeps the
   old form. Over 8000 mpmath-checked pf/pt/pbinom cases the double and
   long double results are as good as before or better, except one pbinom
   tail of 1.6e-15 whose error went from 1.6e-14 to 7e-14 relative; the
   __float128 results are unchanged. pf near the mean at df ~ 1e12, where x
   and y are already rounded separately, is not fixed and is the same in R.

 [Speed]

 - csort() on a hash of arrays rebuilt each column with av_fetch(), newSVsv()
   and av_push() per cell. A column that is not magical is now read through
   AvARRAY() and written into a pre-extended array; a magical column or cell
   takes the general path, with the array and cell held across the FETCH.
   The same cell copy serves the AoA and AoH outputs, and the arrays being
   built are owned while they are filled, so a croak in a FETCH frees them.
   1e6 rows x 5 columns, HoA to HoA, fastest of 5 fresh processes: 0.631 s ->
   0.392 s; peak RSS delta unchanged at 70 MB.
 - qcut() called a Perl closure per element to find NaN/undef cells; the test
   is now written out in the three loops. 1e6 values: 0.185 s -> 0.110 s,
   peak RSS delta 7.6 MB either way.
 - read_table() reads an archive's central directory once per call and
   reuses it for every member lookup. A workbook of 5,000 worksheets read
   in 6.8 s, quadratic in the sheet count, and reads in 0.32 s.
 - qt() in the far tail grew its bracket by doubling: 16384 steps on a
   __float128 perl for qt(1e-300, 0.01), which is -Inf, 102 ms against
   48 us on a double. The bracket now grows by squaring and stops at the
   first point where the tail is still above the target, so that case is
   0.4 ms there and qt(-1e5, 1e3, log_p => 1), whose answer is 1e43,
   went from 1.1 ms to 0.2 ms. qf() and pbinom() on __float128 remain
   slow: they are 130 bisection steps and one soft-float incomplete beta.
 - lm_design_build() ordered terms by looping to the formula's total
   component count, not to its largest degree: `v1*...*v14` took 1.9 s
   in this step alone and four times as long for each variable added.
   It loops to the largest degree, and the margin search starts at the
   first term that can hold the margin. `v1*...*v13` fits in 0.40 s
   where it took 0.52 s; the rest of that time is the formula algebra.

 [Internal]

 - Removed the unused macros nv_sinh, nv_cosh (and sinhl/coshl from the
   link probe in dist.ini and Makefile.PL) and DP_INDEX. NVK_PI,
   NVK_LN_2PI, NVK_LN_SQRT_2PI, NVK_1_SQRT_2PI, NVK_2_SQRT_PI, NVK_EULER,
   NVK_LN2 and PG_KADD stay: they are used on long double and quadmath
   builds, so a double build's -Wunused-macros reports them wrongly.
   AGC_LAST and DENS_K_OPTCOSINE stay as the last members of their lists.

 [Tests]

 - New t/rank.R.scipy.t, with t/rank.R.scipy.py, takes R 4.6.1's and
   SciPy 1.18.0's rank cases (reg-tests-1a.R, rank.Rd, test_rank.py);
   t/rank.t was hand-written and never took them.
 - New t/numeric.options.t calls each function above with each option set

   time: 20000 event times and 1000 groups took 10.6 s. An off-diagonal

   formats a plain number and leaves the string cached on it for good:
   Lonly() of two 1e6-element double arrays grew the process by 304 MB
   that was never returned. They now use uniq()'s key table and render
   a bare number into a stack buffer. On 1e6 doubles get_union() went
   from 1.48 s and +466 MB to 0.41 s and +61 MB. Results are unchanged,

   PVNV with a cached string.

   38 MB per million rows. The label is now rendered without touching

 [group_by()]

 - The mortal key made for each filter of each row lived until the call
   returned, about 16 bytes per row per filter. Each row now has its
   own tmps scope.

 [hoh2hoa()]

   hash lookup for every cell, about 7% on 200000 rows x 10 columns.

 [read_table()]

 - An .xlsx text node holding many '&' and no ';' was read in quadratic
   time, because every '&' scanned the whole remainder for a ';'
   (4e5 '&' in one cell took 0.84 s). The search now stops at the next
   '&', in 0.007 s. What is decoded is unchanged.
 - A .gz or .bz2 file is now read a block at a time, as documented. It
   was not: each 64 KB block of decompressed text was left as a
   temporary until the whole file had been parsed, so a compressed read
   held the entire decompressed text on top of the table. A filtered
   read that kept 20,475 of a 400 MB CSV's 7.8 million rows peaked at
   30 MB from the plain file and at 422 MB from its .gz; a 13 MB CSV
   keeping 300 rows peaked at 14.2 MB from its .gz and now peaks at
   2.2 MB (17.4 MB to 5.1 MB from its .bz2). The blocks are freed as
   each line is read. What is returned is unchanged.

   a CSV or TSV read, as an .xlsx's shared strings already did, so a
   column of categories costs one buffer per value instead of one per
   cell. A 300,000-row CSV with four category columns of six went from
   233 MB to 197 MB as an aoh and from 140 MB to 103 MB as a hoa, and
   about 10% faster (0.109 s to 0.092 s as a hoa). A column whose
   cells do not repeat is noticed and left alone: a 30,000 x 50 file
   of distinct numbers reads in the same time to within 2 ms. The
   values are unchanged, and a write to one cell reaches no other;
   on perls before 5.18 Internals::SvREADONLY() is true of a shared
   cell, as it already was of an .xlsx's. Not for a read with a
   'filter', whose rows are built as before.
 - A field that is an integer written as perl prints one ("42", "-7",
   "0") is now stored as that integer rather than as its text, in every
   kind of read: delimited, .xlsx, filtered, and the values of an
   exploded VCF. It takes 24 bytes where the text took about 72. A
   300,000 x 6 CSV of counts read as a hoa went from 140 MB to 57 MB
   and from 0.110 s to 0.061 s; a 300,000 x 5 CSV with one id column
   from 106 MB to 92 MB. The cell prints as the bytes the file held, so
   eq, hash keys, regexes, sort and write_table() see no difference.
   What does change is anything that looks at a scalar's type: a JSON
   encoder now writes 5 where it wrote "5". Text an integer would not
   print back as is left alone: "007", "+5", "-0", "5.0", "1e3", " 5",
   and a number outside perl's integer range, which is not made a
   float. colClasses => 'character' keeps a column, or every column,
   as text; until now 'character' and no class at all meant the same.

 [write_table()]

 - LaTeX output is written as the records arrive instead of being
   copied into SVs first: a 20 x 200000 table of doubles peaked at
   487 MB and now peaks at 153 MB, as csv does. The bytes written are
   unchanged, and a table with no columns is still refused before the
   file is opened. A croak from the data after the header (a tied cell
   whose FETCH dies) now leaves the partial file, as csv and .xlsx
   already did, where the old file was previously left untouched.
 - An .xlsx sheet now has its top row frozen by default, so the header
   stays in view while scrolling: xlsx_freeze_rows defaults to 1 where
   it defaulted to 0. Pass xlsx_freeze_rows => 0 for a sheet with
   nothing frozen. Giving xlsx_freeze_cols alone therefore freezes the
   header row as well as those columns. This changes the bytes of every
   workbook written without the option; what read_table() reads back
   from it is unchanged.

 [qnorm(), qt(), qchisq(), qf() and qtukey() with log_p]

 - Every q* function exponentiated a log p before inverting it, so a log p
   near 0 rounded to 1 and one below -745 to 0: qnorm(-1e-20, log_p => 1) was
   Inf for R's 9.2623400897984052, qt(-1000, 5, log_p => 1) was -Inf for
   -1.13331635e+87, and qchisq(-1000, 5, log_p => 1) was 0 for
   6.1925242751513702e-174. Each now inverts the smaller of the two tails,
   reflecting a log p above log(1/2) through -expm1(), and solves in logs
   where the probability underflows. qnorm takes R's own asymptotic formulas
   there. Where these q* functions and R's differ by more than 1e-12, mpmath
   at 60 digits sides with this module: R's qt(-700, 5, log.p = TRUE) is
   1.8e-9 off, and its qf(-64, 1, 1, log.p = TRUE) is 0 for
   6.3466722361887189e-56.

 - qt() near the median inverts the central probability 1 - 2p, and takes the
   closed forms for df = 1 and 2 in the tail, as R's qt.c does. qt(1/2 +
   2^-25, 2) was 8.429369701354e-08 where R's own tests/d-p-q-r-tst-2.R pins
   8.429369702179e-08.

 - qf() bisects whichever of t and 1 - t is smaller at the root. It used to
   choose by p alone, which fails when one df dwarfs the other: qf(0.975, 3,
   1e15) was 3.1086244689504672 for 3.1161345348320483.

 [dnorm()]

 - log => 1 returned 0 -- log density 0, density 1 -- wherever the density is
   0: dnorm(Inf, log => 1), dnorm(1, sd => 0, log => 1) and dnorm(0, sd =>
   Inf, log => 1). They are -Inf now, as in R.

 [ptukey() and qtukey()]

 - ptukey() of a NaN was 1, or 0 for the upper tail; it is NaN, as in R.
   qtukey() took a p outside [0, 1] as the nearer end, so qtukey(1.5, 3, 10)
   was Inf and qtukey(-0.1, 3, 10) was 0; it is NaN, as the other q*
   functions return it. The upper tail on the log scale is formed with
   log1p() and -expm1(), as R forms it.

 [pnorm(), dnorm() and the rest of the distribution family]

 - An undef was read as 0, so pnorm([undef]) was [0.5] where R's pnorm(NA) is
   NA; it is NaN, as the README has always said and as the rest of the family
   reads it. Tied elements are fetched once.

 - The result array of pnorm(), dnorm() and the other eight leaked when
   reading an element died -- a tied FETCH, or "isn't numeric" made fatal by
   use warnings FATAL => 'all'. It is mortal before the first element is read
   now.

 [pbinom()]

 - A size that was not exactly whole was NaN, so pbinom(3, 10 + 1e-10, 0.5)
   had no answer where R gives 0.17187500000000006. R's own fuzz, 1e-9 *
   max(1, |size|), is taken now, and the size rounded. A q just below 0 is 0
   now, as R tests q < 0 before its 1e-7 fudge: pbinom(-1e-8, 10, 0.5) used
   to answer for 0.

 [zerotrunc() and hurdle()]

 - A negative-binomial fit to counts no more dispersed than a Poisson's
   returned NaN for every coefficient, standard error and log-likelihood.
   Such a likelihood rises all the way to theta = Inf, so Newton walked
   log(theta) up by about 1 a step until theta * theta overflowed.
   `zerotrunc(y ~ x, dist => 'negbin')` on y = (1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2,
   2, 3), x = 1..12 was all NaN after 500 iterations. The Poisson limit is
   now fitted first, and when the score for overdispersion there is not
   positive that fit is the answer, with `theta` and `SE_logtheta` both Inf:
   intercept -0.4454338 and log-likelihood -13.0227811 on that data, which is
   countreg's Poisson fit. countreg's negbin stops BFGS at theta = 103103 on
   its way there, with -0.4454419 and -13.0228175. The degrees of freedom
   still count theta, as countreg's do. The same check covers a negbin count
   part and a negbin zero part of `hurdle`, whose zero half used to report
   theta_zero near 1e17 where pscl stops at 6.8e4.

 - The derivatives of the negative-binomial likelihood are formed from
   theta/(theta + mu) and mu/(theta + mu) rather than theta * theta, so a
   very large but finite theta no longer overflows them.

   algorithm, as R's fisher.test answers them. The test used to enumerate

   because FEXACT merges paths whose weights agree to 3.45e-7. "As or more

   of a field and the separator written after it, and such a field was not
   quoted: with sep "::" the fields "a:" and ":b" were written "a::::b",

   column holding one as already in order: [3, NaN, 1, 2] came back

   group used to scan every row twice, which was O(groups x rows): 200,000
   rows in 5,000 groups took 1.15 s and take 0.14 s now. Two groups cost
   what they did.

   skips groups with nobody left at risk, and no longer allocates a buffer at
   every event time. 20,000 rows in 500 groups took 1.30 s and take 0.66 s.
   The terms summed are the same ones, and the statistic is bit for bit what
   it was.

   whichever tail it was given. It bisected, against an incomplete gamma that
   itself cost O(sqrt(df)) terms near the median: qchisq(0.5, 1e10) took 11
   ms a call and takes 2.2 us, and qchisq(0.5, 1e15) took 0.26 s and takes
   7.7 us. qchisq(0.95, 3) went from 8.6 us to 1.5 us. Each timing is a fresh
   process per variant on perl-5.44.0.

   it; the name is formatted only when the cell is bad. A 1000 x 1000 table
   took 0.155 s and takes 0.049 s, a 500 x 500 hash of hashes 0.065 s and
   0.029 s, and a million-cell goodness-of-fit vector 0.160 s and 0.040 s. A
   cell named by a UTF-8 hash key is now named as that string rather than as

   look up. h2aoh() already refused reference values for the same reason.
   An object that overloads its operators is still a key, under its string
   form, and is now stringified once per row instead of twice; so is a
   qr//, under its pattern.

 - aoh2h() takes a blessed array of rows, and blessed rows. It refused
   both as "not a hashref", although aoh2hoa() takes them.

 - aoh2h()'s duplicate-key message now names the row, as its other
   messages about a row do and as the documentation said they all did:
   "duplicate key 'a' has >= 2 occurrences, the first repeat at index 2".

 - An undef option name, as in aoh2h($aoh, undef, 1) or h2aoh(\%h, undef,
   1), now dies with "an option name is undefined". It died with perl's
   "Use of uninitialized value within @_ in list assignment at
   .../LikeR.pm line 1169", which named a line of the module rather than
   the mistake.

 [aoh2h(): speed and memory]

 - aoh2h() is now XS. It runs 2.1 to 3.9 times as fast, and its result
   takes 25% to 66% less memory, mostly because the keys are no longer
   also stored in perl's shared string table: a frame's keys are its data,
   and usually live in this one hash. A number is copied as a number, so
   one that has been printed no longer brings its cached string along.
   A tied frame sees the same EXISTS and FETCH calls, in the same order,
   as before. The input is not changed.

 - Each figure below is one cold call on perl 5.44.0, the median of 7
   runs, on a frame of three columns; memory is the RSS the result adds.
   The string values are numeric strings, which is what read_table()
   gives, and the "printed" integers had been interpolated into a string
   before the call. With 1000 distinct keys the result is under 1 MB
   either way.

 [cohen_d()]

 - The confidence interval is now effectsize's noncentral-t interval, the
   exact one under normality: t = d / sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2) on n1 + n2 - 2 df,
   and the limits of its noncentrality parameter, each scaled back by
   sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2). It was d +- z * se, a large-sample interval that is
   too narrow in small samples and matched neither R package: on
   effectsize 1.0.3's own test case, mtcars' weight by transmission, 0.3217
   gave 1.048 to 2.737 where that test pins 1.030 to 2.732. ci_method =>
   'normal' still gives the old interval, and the result's new ci_method
   says which one it holds.

 - Each limit is one root, in the noncentrality, of the same exact_pnt()
   that power_t_test() uses, and agrees with mpmath at 60 digits to
   8.4e-13. The same limits taken from R's pt() are good to about 2e-10,
   and past |ncp| = 37.62 pt() returns a normal approximation: iris's
   upper limits, Sepal.Length against Sepal.Width, are up to 1.6e-3 off in
   R, so the test pins them to mpmath instead.

 [cramers_v()]

 - A table whose total is 1, or below 1 with fractional counts, is now
   refused with "cramers_v: the table total must be more than 1". Bergsma's
   bias correction divides by N - 1, and a total of 1 died on perl's own
   "Illegal division by zero", naming a line of the module.

 [eta_squared()]

 - Group labels that look like numbers are now a factor. The raw form,
   eta_squared(\@values, \@groups), passed aov() a formula, and aov() fits
   a numeric column as one slope, so groups coded 1, 2, 3 were a linear
   trend on 1 df. R's airquality example, Ozone by Month 5 to 9, gave
   eta_sq 0.0271 where summary(aov(Ozone ~ factor(Month))) gives 0.2352.
   The raw form's term is now 'Group', not '__group'.

 - An aov() result with more than one effect term is now refused. It was
   answered for whichever term sorted first, with that term's sum of
   squares plus the residual one taken as the total, so eta_sq was
   partial eta-squared and omega_sq was wrong as well.

 - The raw form fits through oneway_test(var_equal => 1) where the data
   allow it, and through aov() where oneway_test() would refuse them: one
   group, a group of one value, or a value that is undef or not a number.
   On 1e6 values in 5 groups that is 0.10 s and 47 MB, where aov() takes
   0.73 s and 326 MB, and the two agree to 7e-16.

 [hosmer_lemeshow()]

 - The groups and the degrees of freedom are now those of hoslem.test() in
   ResourceSelection 0.3-6. The breaks were not made unique, so a
   prediction tied at the lowest one, as every prediction from a model
   with only categorical predictors is, became a group of its own; and df
   was g - 2 where hoslem.test() has G - 2, for the G groups that hold a
   row. On predictions from a 4-level factor at the default g = 10, 0.3217
   gave X-squared 2.745 on 4 groups and df 8, where hoslem.test() gives
   0.920 on 3 groups and df 1.

 - Fewer groups than g now warn, as R does: "hosmer_lemeshow: the data
   allowed 3 of the 10 groups requested". One group, where R stops, is an
   error.

 - Two departures from hoslem.test() are deliberate, in cases where it has
   no usable answer. A cell whose observed and expected counts are both 0
   adds 0, where R adds 0/0 and returns NaN; that is every cell of an empty
   bin. The last break is the largest prediction: R's seq(0, 1, 1/g) falls
   short of 1 at g = 49, and the package's own example then bins 499 of
   its 500 rows and reports df 48.

 - g must now be an integer; g => 3.5 used to be accepted.

 [smd()]

 - A column that is one constant in both groups now has an SMD of 0, and
   one that is constant within each group but differs between them is
   +-Inf, as in tableone 0.13.2's StdDiff(). Both died with "pooled
   standard deviation is zero", so one constant covariate took a whole
   balance table down.

 [table_one()]

 - A continuous variable whose test cannot run now gets no p-value, as a
   categorical one already did. t_test() dies on data that are constant
   and on a group of one observation, and that took the whole table down.

 - A by column with a group named variable, level, type, p_value, test or
   Overall is now an error. Each group is a key of every output row, so a
   group named 'test' had its summary overwritten by the label 't-test',
   and one named 'Overall' overwrote the column that summarises every row.

 - A types value other than 'continuous' or 'categorical' is now an error.
   types => { age => 'numeric' } was taken as categorical, a row for every
   distinct age.

 - A by column shorter than the frame now reads as NA past its end, as
   every other column did; it died on perl's "uninitialized value"
   warning. A categorical column shorter than the frame now lists its rows
   past the end as an NA level. They were already counted in the
   percentages.

 - Levels that are all numbers are listed in numeric order, with NA last.
   They were sorted as strings, so stage 10 came between 1 and 2.

 [table_one(): speed and memory]

 - Columns are fetched one at a time instead of all at once; each value is
   made a number once, where mean(), sd() and the test each parsed their
   own copy of the string; the per-row group label strings and level
   strings are gone; and with more than two groups the ANOVA p-value comes
   from oneway_test(var_equal => 1), which agrees with aov() to the 1e-12
   that R's anova(lm()) and oneway.test() differ by on the same data.

 - Each figure is the best of 3 cold calls on perl 5.44.0 with by => 'arm'
   (three groups) over four continuous and four categorical columns, about
   5% missing; memory is the peak RSS the call adds.

 - | rows | frame | test | time, 0.3217 -> 0.3218 | memory, 0.3217 -> 0.3218 |

   | 1e6 | AoH | parametric | 10.53 s -> 5.32 s | 1573.7 MB -> 536.8 MB |
   | 1e6 | AoH | nonparametric | 7.40 s -> 5.56 s | 1416.7 MB -> 545.0 MB |
   | 1e6 | HoA | parametric | 8.71 s -> 2.72 s | 748.2 MB -> 167.0 MB |
   | 1e6 | HoA | nonparametric | 5.55 s -> 2.94 s | 590.5 MB -> 172.6 MB |

   | 1e5 | HoA | parametric | 0.72 s -> 0.23 s | 75.5 MB -> 16.8 MB |

 [vif()]

 - vif() is now car 3.1-5's vif() at its default type = "terms", computed
   on the design lm() builds from the formula. It split the right-hand
   side on '+' and regressed each piece on the others, so y ~ x1*x2 + x3,
   y ~ x1 + x2 - x3, y ~ ., y ~ x1 + x2 - 1 and any factor died, with
   lm()'s "0 degrees of freedom" or with "need at least two predictors".
   All of those now work. A term with more than one column, such as a
   factor of three or more levels, gets car's generalized VIF, and each
   term then maps to { GVIF, Df, 'GVIF^(1/(2*Df))' }, as car's result
   becomes a table. When every term has one column the result is the hash
   of numbers it always was.

 - A formula's response now takes out the rows where it is missing, as it
   does from car's model; it was ignored. On airquality's Ozone ~ Solar.R
   + Wind + Temp that is car's 111 rows rather than 146, and Solar.R's VIF
   goes from 1.0893 to car's 1.0953. A response that is not a column of
   the data is an error naming it, where it used to be ignored. An array
   of names, or a formula with no response, uses every row that has the
   predictors, as before.

 - car's warnings and refusals have counterparts: "there are higher-order
   terms (interactions) in this model", "No intercept: vifs may not be
   sensible.", "model contains fewer than 2 terms" (which was "need at
   least two predictors"), and "there are aliased coefficients in the
   model", now naming the column. An aliased column used to get a VIF of
   Inf.

 [Formulas: lm(), glm(), anova(), aov() and the rest]

 - A term can now be removed with '-', as in R: y ~ x*z - x:z is y ~ x +
   z, y ~ . - id is every column but id, and - x*z takes out x, z and x:z.
   The parser split only on '+', so "z-w" was looked up as one column, no
   row had it, and the fit died with "0 degrees of freedom". A '-' inside
   parentheses is not removal, and a term that names a column is still
   that column, so y ~ a-b fits a column named a-b as it did.

 - A formula crossing seven or more variables with '*', which has 128 or
   more terms, wrote past the end of the parser's list of distinct terms:
   it was allocated at 64 beside the list of all terms, and only the latter
   grew as a cross was expanded. valgrind reported the invalid writes in
   lm() on y ~ a*b*c*d*e*f*g; the list is now sized once the count is
   known. Every function that reads a formula through lm()'s parser was
   affected: lm(), glm(), anova(), aov(), coxph(), zerotrunc(), hurdle(),
   svyglm(), ivreg() and lmer().

 [pchisq() and qchisq()]

 - df => 0 is now the chi-square with all its mass at 0, as in R:
   pchisq($q, 0) is 0 for $q <= 0 and 1 above, and qchisq($p, 0) is 0, or
   Inf at $p = 1. Both returned NaN, and t/distributions.R.scipy.t asserted
   NaN for pchisq(1, 0) under a comment saying R returns NaN there too. R's
   own tests/d-p-q-r-tst-2.R pins the values above.

0.3217 2026-10-12 CDT 

 [cor()]

 - Spearman and Kendall correlations with a missing value now return NaN,
   as R's cor() does at its default use = "everything". They used to rank
   or count the NaN like any other value and return a finite, meaningless
   answer: cor([1,2,undef,4,5,6], [2,1,4,3,6,5], 'spearman') was 0.82857,
   which is neither R's NA nor the complete-case 0.8, and 'kendall' was
   0.6. Pearson already returned NaN. The same holds for every entry of a
   correlation matrix that involves a column with a missing value.

 - A y that is neither an array reference nor undef now croaks. It used to
   be taken for "no y", so cor(\@x, 'spearman'), with the method in y's
   place, returned 1. The method is the third argument: cor(\@x, undef,
   'spearman').

 - A matrix x with a y that is not a matrix now croaks. cor($X, \@v) and
   cor($X, []) both used to drop y without a word and return cor($X). R
   answers the first with a p x 1 matrix; this refuses rather than guess.

 - A one-row matrix is now told it needs at least 2 observations. It used
   to be told that its column 0 had zero variance.

 - Pearson no longer overflows or underflows on data far from 1 on a double
   perl. 1e90 * c(0,0,0,1,1,1,1) against 1e90 * 0:6 returned 0 where R and
   SciPy give 0.8660254037844386, and SciPy's very-small-input case (y
   down to 2e-245) returned NaN where they give 0.727293054075045. A
   column whose sum of squares overflows or loses bits to underflow is now
   divided by its largest deviation first, which leaves r unchanged, and
   the denominator takes each root separately when their product would
   leave the range. Ordinary data never reaches either branch and gives the
   same bits.
   SciPy's extremely-large case now gives its 0.351312332103289, where R's
   own cor() gives NA.

 - t/cor.R.scipy.t cross-checks cor() against R 4.6.1's regression tests
   and cor.Rd examples and SciPy's TestPearsonr, TestCorrSpearmanr,
   TestKendallTau and TestSpearmanRho: 1430 checks, covering every method
   in vector, matrix and cross-matrix form, missing values, ties, and a
   200,000-pair Kendall case whose pair count passes 2**32. It is what
   found the overflow above.

 [cor_test()]

 - The documented call form cor_test(x => \@x, y => \@y, ...) now works.
   Only cor_test(\@x, \@y, ...) was parsed, so the named form croaked
   "unknown argument 'y'". Both are accepted and give the same result;
   t/cor_test.call_forms.t checks them against each other under every
   method and alternative.

 - The documentation now says how missing values, the y argument and the
   cases that differ from R on purpose behave.

 [cor(), cov() and cor_test(): speed and memory]

 - A correlation matrix is faster: 2.8 to 5.4 times, measured on
   perl-5.44.0. Pearson centred both columns of every pair afresh, so each
   column was centred once per partner; each column is now centred once
   and a pair costs a single pass, four pairs to a sweep. Kendall sorted
   every pair by both columns; each column is now sorted once and only its
   runs of ties are re-sorted per partner. A 2000 x 400 matrix went from
   0.24 s to 0.047 s for Pearson and from 0.28 s to 0.075 s for Spearman;
   a 1000 x 60 Kendall matrix went from 0.21 s to 0.075 s, and a 2000-row
   Pearson cross-correlation of 200 columns against 200 went from 0.12 s
   to 0.023 s. Every entry is bit-for-bit what it was.

 - Kendall's tau is 1.6 times faster and needs half the scratch memory.
   The y tie counts now come from the merge sort's own output instead of a
   separate sort of y, the merge no longer copies its result back at every
   level, and its scratch is carved out of the pair array once the x
   values are spent. At n = 1e6, cor(), cov() and cor_test() with method
   'kendall' each went from 0.26 s to 0.17 s, and peak memory above the
   input from 46.6 MB to 31.2 MB.

 - A Spearman correlation of two vectors ranks them in place, which cut
   peak memory above the input from 46.5 MB to 31.3 MB at n = 1e6.

 [filter()]

 - A col() predicate naming a column the frame does not have now dies,
   "filter: column 'agee' not found in data", as R's subset() does. It
   used to read undef in every row, so col('agee') > 18 kept nothing and
   !(col('agee') > 18) kept everything, without a word. A column only some
   rows of an AoH or HoH carry is still a column; an AoH or HoH with no
   rows is not checked. Each predicate records the columns it reads in
   {cols}. A code reference names none and is not checked.

 - && || and or between col() predicates now die. A predicate's truth
   value was 1, so col('a') > 4 && col('b') < 2 quietly became
   col('b') < 2. Combine with & | !.

 - col('x') > col('y') now dies rather than keeping every row with a
   numeric x: the cell was compared with the col object, whose own
   overloaded > returned a true predicate. Compare two columns in a sub.

 - The result no longer shares the input's reference SVs, only the rows
   they point to, so $out->[0] = undef no longer emptied $df->[0], for an
   AoH and for a HoH.

 - $_ and $_[0] in a predicate are a reference made for the call. They
   were the frame's own, so $_ = undef in a predicate cleared the caller's
   AoH row, and on a HoA freed the row buffer and crashed perl.

 - A predicate that deletes its own row from a HoH, or a column from a
   HoA, no longer crashes perl; and one that deletes a cell of the HoA row
   buffer, keeps it and stores another under the same name no longer has
   every later row written into the cell it kept.

 - An integer cell and literal compare exactly when either is a UV:
   col('x') <= 9223372036854775807 kept a cell of 9223372036854775808,
   both rounding to 2**63 as doubles.

 - A string comparison FETCHes a tied cell once, not twice, on perl 5.14
   and later.

 - A cell that is an object with overloaded operators, such as a
   Math::BigInt, is compared by its own class, as a sub predicate compares
   it. The compiled col() test took it for a non-number, so col('x') > 2
   dropped a Math::BigInt 5 that the same test written as a sub kept, and
   a string comparison used its stringification instead of its cmp. Such
   a row is now handed to the predicate's Perl closure; the others stay in
   C, and a frame with no such cells runs exactly as fast as before.

 [filter(): speed and memory]

 - Converting an AoH or HoH to a HoA no longer gives every row of the
   input an iterator. perl allocates one on a hash's first iteration and
   never frees it, so filtering a 200000-row, two-column AoH to a HoA
   left it at 70.3 MB where it had been 47.4 MB, and the peak above the
   input for 1e6 one-column rows was 197 MB. It is 20.5 MB now, and the
   input is unchanged. The rows are also read once each rather than once
   per column, and AoH -> HoA runs in about half the time: 119 ms to 59 ms
   for a col() predicate on 300000 rows of 5 columns, 162 ms to 91 ms for
   a sub. HoH -> HoA went from 397 ms to 303 ms.

 - A sub predicate's row index or row name ($_[1]) is freed after each
   row. It used to be held until filter() returned, so the peak above the
   input for a 1e6-row AoH went from 35.3 MB to 16.3 MB, and for a HoH
   from 66.1 MB to 31.5 MB.

 [roc(), auc() and auroc()]

 - A NaN score no longer hangs roc(). Every comparison against a NaN is
   false, so the threshold sweep stood still on one and pushed a new curve
   point on every pass until memory ran out: roc([1,"nan",3,4],[0,0,1,1])
   never returned. auc() and auroc() returned whatever the sort made of the
   NaN, so the same cases in a different order gave 0, 0.333 or 0.667. A
   missing score (undef, NaN or a hole) or a missing label (undef or a
   hole) now drops its case, as pROC's roc() does with na.rm = TRUE, its
   default. An undef score used to be read as 0 and an undef label as a
   negative. n, n_pos and n_neg count the cases that were used.

 - roc() with direction => '<' reports its thresholds on the scores' own
   scale. They were reported negated: roc([4,3,2,1], [0,0,1,1], direction
   => '<') put the Youden cut at -2 rather than 2, and its curve ran from
   +Inf down through -1 .. -4. The curve now runs from -Inf up through the
   scores, and a case is called positive when its score is at or below the
   threshold.

 - auc_se and auc_ci are NaN when either class has a single case, as
   pROC's var() and ci.auc() are NA. The DeLong variance is undefined there,
   and they used to be 0 and an interval collapsed onto the AUC.

 - A score that is not a number croaks, naming its index, as does a truth
   value that is not a number in auroc()'s cutoff and active_frac modes.
   Both used to be read as 0. A direction other than '>' or '<', and a
   trailing key with no value, croak too; only the first character of
   direction was read, and a dangling key was ignored.

 - auroc()'s cutoff and active_frac modes drop a case whose truth value is
   NaN. active_frac handed it to qsort(), which cannot order a NaN, so the
   set of actives it chose depended on where the NaN sat in the input.
   Equal truth values at the edge of the fraction are now taken in input
   order on every platform.

 - A label is positive when it is eq to positive. A label and positive
   holding the same character, one as UTF-8 and the other as bytes, used
   to be compared byte for byte and count as different.

 - Nothing is leaked when a call dies part way: the buffers are released
   on the save stack. A label whose string overload died used to leak 1.5
   MB per call on 200,000 cases.

 - roc() is about 5 times faster and auc() about 3 times faster, and both
   use about a sixth of the memory: on 2,000,000 cases on perl-5.44.0, roc()
   went from 0.69 s to 0.13 s and auc() from 0.39 s to 0.12 s, and the peak
   above the input from 203 MB to 31 MB for each. The cases are sorted once
   and the AUC and the DeLong placement values come from one walk over the
   tie groups, where three rank sorts and six scratch arrays were used
   before. 0/1 labels are no longer stringified in place, which left a
   cached string on every label of the caller's array. The AUC is now the
   exact count ratio rounded once; it used to differ from that in the 13th
   digit at this size.

 - t/roc.R.t checks all three against pROC 1.19.0.1 on pROC's own aSAH data
   (its test-auc.R, test-var.R, test-ci.auc.R and test-roc.R values, and
   every point of each curve) and against scikit-learn 1.9.1's
   test_roc_curve_toydata. t/roc.R.R regenerates its reference block.

 [bedroc()]

 - A NaN score no longer hangs bedroc(): its tie-group walk stood still on
   one, as roc()'s did. A missing score or label now drops its case, as in
   roc(); an undef score used to be read as 0 and an undef label as
   inactive. Labels compare with positive as eq does, and a direction other
   than '>' or '<', or a dangling key, croaks.

 - Under cutoff and active_frac, a NaN truth value drops its case. It used
   to reach qsort(), which cannot order a NaN: over 300 shuffles of one
   9-row input, active_frac gave 45 different answers. Under cutoff it
   counted as inactive.

 - The score is right for every alpha. Truchon & Bayly's eq. 36 cancels as
   alpha shrinks and overflows as it grows, so on scores 6..1 with labels
   [1,0,1,0,0,0] it gave 1200.75 at alpha = 1e-6, Inf at 1e-8 and NaN at
   1500, where the exact values are 0.875, 0.875 and 1. It is now evaluated
   in an algebraically equal form, written as one minus the shortfall from
   the ideal ranking, that does neither; rie, rie_min and rie_max likewise.
   t/bedroc.mpmath.t checks all four against the paper's formula in mpmath
   at 60 digits from alpha = 1e-8 to 1500, with a worst error of one ulp.

 - top => enrichment no longer depends on the input order of tied scores.
   A tie group that straddles the cut counts its actives in proportion to
   how much of it is inside, so bedroc([5,5,5,5], [1,0,0,0], top => 0.25)
   and the same with labels [0,0,0,1] both report 0.25, where they were 1
   and 0. active_count can therefore be fractional.

 [rbinom(), rnorm(), runif()]

 - rbinom(prob => 'nan') no longer hangs; like R it returns NaN for every
   draw, with the warning "NAs produced", as it does for a size that is not
   a whole number (2.5 used to draw from size 2). A prob that is not a
   number croaks, where it was read as 0, and n is required, where omitting
   it returned [].

 - rnorm() takes its arguments as runif() does: rnorm(1e3), rnorm("5") and
   R's own rnorm(10, 0, 1) used to croak, because a positional n had to
   test as an integer. A mean or sd that is not a number croaks.

 - rnorm(sd => Inf) and runif(n, 0, Inf) are NaN with a warning, as in R;
   they were +-Inf and Inf. rnorm() with sd => 0 or an infinite mean
   returns the mean, as R does.

 - rbinom() and hist() no longer hang when given more than 65535
   arguments: their argument loops counted in an unsigned short.

 [mean(), sum(), median(), var(), sd()]

 - The sum behind sum(), mean(), var() and sd() is compensated (TwoSum),
   which is what R gets from accumulating in long double:
   mean([1e16, 1, -1e16, 1]) is 0.5 and sum() of it 2, where both used to be
   0. It costs about 0.5 ns per element: on perl-5.44.0, one pinned core,
   sum() of 1e6 NVs went from 0.93 to 1.40 ns per element.

 - A sum that overflows although no value is infinite is taken again with
   each value scaled by 1/n, so mean([1e308, 1e308]) is 1e308 and var() and
   sd() of it 0, as in R; they were Inf, NaN and NaN. median() halves the
   middle pair before adding it when the sum would overflow.

   var([1e200, -1e200, 3e199]) was NaN, from Inf - Inf.

   count is at least 0.5 from its expectation, as mantelhaen.test() does,
   and its method says "with" or "without" accordingly.

   off-diagonal counts has a common odds ratio of Inf, not NaN. A NaN or
   infinite cell croaks, in epi_2x2() too, whose scalar form also croaks on

   only, so a level seen just in a dropped pair no longer enlarges the
   table: one such case gave df 3 and p 0.9536 where R gives df 1 and p 1.

   undef and non-numeric cells croak, where Inf passed and the others were
   read as 0, and the exact test croaks on a fractional count rather than
   truncating it.

   dropped, as R drops it; an undef was read as 0. A dangling key croaks.

   'greater' croaks; 'bogus' used to run a two-sided test. README now

   back in hash order, which changed with PERL_HASH_SEED.

   other reduction does, where they croaked about zero variance.

   intersection(), Lonly(), Ronly(), is_equivalent() and value_counts() on
   a tied array of hashes now read a tied array. Each tested SvOK() or
   SvROK() before the element's get magic had run, so every element read as
   undef and they croaked.

 - transpose(), sample(), ljoin() and add_data() put copies of the input's
   values in their results. Each stored the caller's own scalars, so
   writing to the result changed the input: transpose($m)->[0][1] = 99
   changed $m, although README says the input is never modified. A
   reference is copied as a reference. transpose() also stores a writable
   undef for a hole, where it stored the read-only PL_sv_undef. Copying
   costs transpose() of a dense 3000 x 100 hash of hashes about 4 ms (18 to
   22 ms).

   pre-sized every column for every row, so a sparse hash of hashes took
   quadratic memory: a 5000-row diagonal peaked at 237 MB and now at 1.8 MB.

   population's whole index array even for n = 1, 40 MB and 11.5 ms a call
   on 5e6 elements, and now keeps the swaps of a small sample in a table;

   and croaks when the C library will not allocate the cells, where eval {
   matrix([1], 1, 1e11) } took perl down with "Out of memory!".

 [Leaks when a call dies part way]

   hist(), density(), bw_ucv(), bw_bcv() and bedroc() release their
   buffers on the save stack. A croak from perl code they call -- an
   overload or a tie that dies, or a $SIG{__WARN__} that dies on their
   warning -- used to leak them: over 40 such calls on the 0.3217 before
   this, 13 to 38 MB each for all but bw_ucv() (1.3 MB). t/croak.leaks.t

   compared against R or mpmath elsewhere, and
   t/friedman_mcnemar_prop_cmh.R.t gains R 4.6.1 rows for the cmh_test(),
   mcnemar_test() and prop_test() cases.

   gives the other shapes, 'row_names' another key, and the new explode => 0
